set_title: CLAT PG Practice Set 05 (Jurisprudence, Legal Theory, Jurisprudential Judgments and the New Criminal Laws; Trap-Annotated)

pattern.ordering: Passages 1-19: jurisprudence, legal theory and the judgments built on them; passages 20-25: mens rea and the new criminal laws (BNS, BNSS)
pattern.note: Practice set, not a mock; original passages and questions (none taken from Mock 01-06 or Practice Sets 01-03). Passages carry verbatim extracts from public-domain jurisprudential texts and Indian judgments; works still in copyright (Hart, Kelsen, Dworkin, Raz, Rawls, Nozick, Honore, Sen, Finnis) appear only as short phrases and paraphrase. The official paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes; this set is longer for extra practice.

Correct answer carries 1 mark; each wrong answer carries -0.25.

Passages are original summaries for practice. Verify quotations against the cited editions and BNS, BNSS section numbers against India Code before publishing; verify pending or evolving matters (e.g. the marital-rape exception challenge, the Sabarimala-type reference matters, the status of the Ganga-Yamuna personhood appeal) against current official sources.
Every explanation includes why the other options fail, the CLAT trap, and any language trick.

passages.title: Natural Law: From Cicero and Aquinas to Finnis
passages.passage: Natural law theory holds that law has a necessary connection with morality. Cicero wrote in De Re Publica that 'True law is right reason in agreement with nature; it is of universal application, unchanging and everlasting.' Aquinas distinguished eternal, natural, human and divine law, and defined law as 'nothing else than an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated.' He added that a human law which 'deflects from the law of nature' is 'no longer a law but a perversion of law'. Yet he did not say that every unjust law may be disobeyed: a law unjust because it runs against the human good does not bind in conscience, save perhaps to avoid scandal or disturbance, whereas a law contrary to the divine good must never be obeyed. Blackstone declared that the law of nature, 'being coeval with mankind and dictated by God himself, is of course superior in obligation to any other', and that no human law is valid if contrary to it. The seventeenth century moved the basis from theology to reason and consent. Grotius held that the law of nature would have some validity even if there were no God. Hobbes, who described the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short', held that 'covenants, without the sword, are but words'. Locke grounded natural rights in life, liberty and estate and wrote that 'where there is no law, there is no freedom'. In the modern revival, John Finnis argues in Natural Law and Natural Rights that there are basic goods, such as life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness and religion, which are self-evident and incommensurable. He treats law as deriving its moral force from the common good, and an unjust law as law only in a defective, non-focal sense, not as a nullity.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of Aquinas's definition of law as given in the passage?

options.A: that it is directed to the common good of the community
options.B: that it is backed by a sanction imposed by a sovereign
options.C: that it is an ordinance of reason and not mere will
options.D: that it is promulgated to those who are bound by it

questions.explanation: Sanction and sovereign belong to Austin's vocabulary. Aquinas's definition lists reason, the common good, lawful authority (him who has care of the community) and promulgation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is an express element of the definition. Option C is an express element, since law is called an ordinance of reason. Option D is an express element, since the definition ends with the word promulgated.
questions.clat_trap: Austin's command-and-sanction vocabulary is planted in the correct option to catch candidates who assume every definition of law is coercive.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' and 'determinate sovereign': the three wrong options are verbatim components of the quoted definition.

questions.question: A statute burdens citizens in a way contrary to the human good, though it does not require anything contrary to divine law. On Aquinas, as stated in the passage, the statute

options.A: does not bind in conscience, though obedience may be prudent to avoid scandal or disturbance
options.B: must be disobeyed in every case, because only divine law can bind a person in conscience
options.C: binds in conscience exactly as a just law does, because it was properly made by authority
options.D: may be disobeyed whenever obedience is inconvenient, since an unjust law is no law at all

questions.explanation: Laws against the human good do not bind in conscience, save perhaps to avoid scandal or disturbance. Only a law contrary to the divine good must never be obeyed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reserves absolute disobedience for laws contrary to the divine good, not for every unjust law. Option C states the positivist view that proper enactment alone secures binding force, which Aquinas denies. Option D turns the slogan that an unjust law is no law into a licence to disobey, which Aquinas qualifies.
questions.clat_trap: The popular slogan lex iniusta non est lex is offered as bait; Aquinas's actual position is more qualified.
questions.language_trick: 'save perhaps to avoid scandal' versus 'whenever obedience is inconvenient'.

questions.question: Finnis's view of an unjust law, as stated in the passage, is closest to the claim that it is

options.A: as fully law as any other, differing from a just law only in merit
options.B: law only in a defective, non-focal sense, and not a nullity
options.C: law only if it can be derived from one of the incommensurable basic goods
options.D: a complete nullity that creates no obligation of any kind

questions.explanation: The passage says Finnis treats an unjust law as law only in a defective, non-focal sense, not as a nullity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the Austinian separation of existence and merit. Option C invents a derivation test; basic goods ground moral force, not a rule's membership of the legal system. Option D attributes to Finnis the strong invalidity thesis that the passage expressly denies.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates fuse Finnis with the Augustinian slogan, or with Austin, and choose one of the extremes.
questions.language_trick: 'defective' and 'not a nullity' sit between 'nullity' and 'fully law'.

questions.question: Consider the following statements based on the passage. 1. Cicero treats true law as local and variable according to custom. 2. Aquinas distinguished eternal, natural, human and divine law. 3. Locke grounded natural rights in life, liberty and estate. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 2 and 3 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statement 1 is false because Cicero describes true law as universal and everlasting. Statements 2 and 3 are stated in the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement 1, which reverses Cicero's claim that true law is of universal application, unchanging and everlasting. Option C includes statement 1 and omits statement 2, which the passage states expressly. Option D includes statement 1, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: One reversed statement is slipped into a block of accurate ones so that a quick reader accepts all three.
questions.language_trick: 'local and variable' against 'universal application, unchanging and everlasting'.

questions.question: Blackstone's statement that no human law is valid if contrary to the law of nature differs from Finnis's treatment of an unjust law because Blackstone

options.A: accepts that an unjust rule is fully valid law, so long as it was properly enacted
options.B: treats the law of nature as a convention that binds only where it is enforced
options.C: derives the law of nature from consent and reason without any reference to God
options.D: denies validity outright, whereas Finnis keeps the unjust rule as defective law

questions.explanation: Blackstone states an invalidity thesis; Finnis, as presented, stops short of it and calls the unjust law defective but still law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses his position, since he says such a law has no validity. Option B is the Hobbesian view of covenants, not Blackstone's. Option C contradicts his description of the law of nature as dictated by God himself.
questions.clat_trap: Both writers are 'natural lawyers', which tempts candidates to merge their positions.

questions.question: Which of the following statements would Hobbes, as presented in the passage, accept?

options.A: A covenant in a state of nature has no strength unless a power exists to compel its performance
options.B: A covenant binds because natural law would be valid even if there were no God to command it
options.C: Natural rights to life, liberty and estate bind everyone independently of any coercive power
options.D: A law lacking enforcement is fully effective if it is reasonable and generally accepted as just

questions.explanation: For Hobbes, covenants without the sword are but words: obligation in the state of nature is empty without a power able to compel.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B attributes the Grotian claim to Hobbes. Option C attributes Locke's position to Hobbes. Option D contradicts the remark that covenants without the sword are but words.
questions.clat_trap: Locke and Grotius are blended into the distractors, tempting candidates to credit Hobbes with their theses.
questions.language_trick: 'without the sword' means 'without a power able to compel'.

passages.title: Bentham, Mill and the Limits of Law
passages.passage: Jeremy Bentham opened An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation with the statement that 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' The principle of utility approves or disapproves of every action according to its tendency to augment or diminish the happiness of the party whose interest is in question; for the community, 'it is the greatest happiness of the greatest number that is the measure of right and wrong'. Bentham proposed a felicific calculus which values a pleasure or pain by its intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity and extent, and he counted only quantity, so that, in the saying attributed to him, pushpin is as good as poetry. He attacked natural rights: 'Natural rights is simple nonsense: natural and imprescriptible rights, rhetorical nonsense,--nonsense upon stilts.' For him, 'Right, the substantive right, is the child of law'. On punishment he wrote that 'all punishment in itself is evil' and should be admitted only 'in as far as it promises to exclude some greater evil'. John Stuart Mill accepted utility but added quality: 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.' In On Liberty (1859) he stated the harm principle: 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.' Conduct that concerns only oneself is outside the reach of law, while conduct affecting others may be regulated. Act utilitarianism applies the principle of utility to each act, while rule utilitarianism applies it to rules whose general observance would maximise welfare.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a dimension used in Bentham's felicific calculus as listed in the passage?

options.A: fecundity, or the chance of being followed by sensations of the same kind
options.B: propinquity, or how near or remote the pleasure or pain is
options.C: purity, or the chance of not being followed by sensations of the opposite kind
options.D: the nobility or quality of the pleasure

questions.explanation: Bentham counted only quantity; the qualitative distinction among pleasures is Mill's addition.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is a listed dimension, measuring the chance of being followed by sensations of the same kind. Option B is a listed dimension, measuring how near or remote the pleasure or pain is. Option C is a listed dimension, measuring the chance of not being followed by sensations of the opposite kind.
questions.clat_trap: Mill's qualitative idea is offered as the odd one out so that candidates credit it to Bentham.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' and 'quality': the passage says Bentham counted only quantity.

questions.question: A citizen claims a 'natural and imprescriptible' right to carry on a trade which a valid statute prohibits. In Bentham's terms, the claim

options.A: is a legal right whenever the trade would add to the happiness of the greatest number
options.B: is rhetorical nonsense, since real rights come only from real laws
options.C: is valid only if it can be traced to reason and consent, as Locke argued
options.D: is a genuine right that overrides the statute because it exists prior to law

questions.explanation: For Bentham a right is the child of law; a claim to a right against all law is an imaginary right drawn from an imaginary law of nature.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A lets utility by itself create a legal right, whereas for Bentham a right is the child of law. Option C borrows Locke's justification, which Bentham's attack rejects. Option D states the natural-rights view that Bentham ridiculed as nonsense upon stilts.
questions.clat_trap: Utility is tempting as the explanation of every Benthamite answer, but he separates what the law ought to be from what rights exist.
questions.language_trick: 'real laws' and 'imaginary laws' in the quoted passage.

questions.question: An adult privately consumes a substance that harms only his own health. The State seeks to punish him for his own good. On Mill's harm principle as quoted, the State

options.A: may do so because the pleasure obtained from the substance is of a lower quality
options.B: may do so if rule utilitarianism approves a general prohibition of the substance
options.C: may not do so, since his own good is no warrant and no harm to others is shown
options.D: may do so if a majority of citizens regards the habit as immoral

questions.explanation: Mill confines coercion to preventing harm to others; the individual's own physical or moral good is not a sufficient warrant.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses Mill's ranking of pleasures with a licence to coerce. Option B imports a welfare test that the harm principle, as stated, does not use to justify coercion of self-regarding conduct. Option D treats majority disapproval as a warrant, which the harm principle rejects.
questions.clat_trap: Mill's higher-and-lower pleasures are placed in a distractor to suggest that low pleasures may be suppressed.
questions.language_trick: 'own good, either physical or moral' is expressly excluded.

questions.question: The main difference between Bentham and Mill on pleasures, according to the passage, is that

options.A: Mill treated natural rights as prior to law, whereas Bentham treated them as legal creations
options.B: Mill added a qualitative distinction among pleasures, whereas Bentham counted only quantity
options.C: Mill rejected the principle of utility altogether, whereas Bentham accepted it
options.D: Bentham stated the harm principle, whereas Mill rejected it

questions.explanation: The passage says Bentham counted only quantity and Mill added quality while accepting utility.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attributes to Mill a natural-rights view the passage does not support. Option C contradicts the statement that Mill accepted utility. Option D attributes the harm principle to the wrong thinker; it is Mill's own.
questions.clat_trap: Both are utilitarians, so candidates exaggerate the difference into a rejection of utility.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Bentham treated punishment as an evil, justified only so far as it promises to exclude some greater evil. 2. Mill's harm principle makes a person's own moral good a sufficient warrant for coercion. 3. Rule utilitarianism tests rules by whether their general observance would maximise welfare. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 3 only
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 restate the passage. Statement 2 contradicts Mill's quoted words that his own good is not a sufficient warrant.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B omits statement 3, which correctly states rule utilitarianism. Option C includes statement 2, which reverses the quoted harm principle. Option D includes statement 2, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: The false statement is the exact negation of a quoted sentence.
questions.language_trick: 'is not a sufficient warrant' becomes 'a sufficient warrant'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Bentham accepted natural and imprescriptible rights as limits on legislation. Reason (R): Bentham called natural rights 'nonsense upon stilts'.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because Bentham rejected natural rights; R is true because the phrase is his.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats A as true, although Bentham rejected natural rights. Option B treats A as true, although Bentham rejected natural rights. Option C treats A as true and R as false, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: R is true and tempting, so candidates assume it must support A.

passages.title: Austin's Province of Jurisprudence and Its Critics
passages.passage: In The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832), John Austin fixed the subject of jurisprudence: 'The matter of jurisprudence is positive law: law, simply and strictly so called: or law set by political superiors to political inferiors.' He held that 'laws or rules, properly so called, are a species of commands', each combining a wish, a sanction and a duty, and he separated the 'is' from the 'ought': 'The existence of law is one thing; its merit and demerit another.' A sovereign is a determinate human superior 'not in a habit of obedience to a like superior' who receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society. Sovereignty is indivisible and legally illimitable, since a legal limit would presuppose a higher sovereign. Austin classed rules into laws of God, positive laws and positive morality; he treated constitutional law and international law as positive morality, because no sovereign sets them, and rules of fashion or honour as laws only by analogy. Custom became law only when adopted by the courts, as a tacit command of the sovereign. Critics responded in several ways. Maine pointed to Ranjit Singh's Punjab, where a powerful ruler issued few general commands while custom governed daily life, to show that the command model ignores customary law. Hart argued that the gunman case shows the difference between being obliged and having an obligation, and that power-conferring rules and the continuity of law-making authority cannot be explained by habits of obedience. Federal systems with divided powers strain the idea of an indivisible sovereign, and written constitutions show that law-making bodies can be legally limited.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT 'law properly so called' on Austin's classification as described in the passage?

options.A: a command of the sovereign to a member of the society, backed by a sanction
options.B: a custom adopted by the courts of the sovereign
options.C: a rule of public international law
options.D: a statute enacted by the sovereign legislature of an independent political society

questions.explanation: Austin classed international law as positive morality, since no sovereign sets it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the paradigm of law properly so called. Option B becomes law as a tacit command of the sovereign once the courts adopt it. Option D is a command set by the sovereign to subjects and so is law properly so called.
questions.clat_trap: International law is known as 'law', so candidates assume it must count as law proper.
questions.language_trick: 'properly so called' is a term of art; positive morality is outside it.

questions.question: A written constitution forbids a State's legislature from abridging a certain freedom, and the legislature does so. On Austin's framework as described, the constitutional prohibition on that sovereign body is

options.A: a tacit command adopted by the courts of the society, and so law properly so called
options.B: a legal duty enforced by a higher sovereign standing above the legislature itself
options.C: a rule of divine law binding the legislature as a limit on its competence
options.D: positive morality, not law proper, as a legal limit would presuppose a higher sovereign

questions.explanation: Because the sovereign is legally illimitable, constitutional restraints on it are positive morality rather than law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses the doctrine on custom with limits on the sovereign. Option B contradicts the premise that the sovereign is indivisible and illimitable. Option C divine law is a separate class in Austin's scheme; constitutional limits are classed as positive morality.
questions.clat_trap: Modern lawyers regard constitutional limits as law, so the Austinian classification feels wrong and candidates reject it.

questions.question: Critics use Ranjit Singh's Punjab chiefly to show that

options.A: law can be largely customary, so law is not reducible to commands of a determinate sovereign
options.B: absolute rulers always make most of the law themselves through general commands
options.C: sovereignty is divisible between a ruler and customary bodies within the same society
options.D: habitual obedience is absent under despotic rulers, so they are not sovereign

questions.explanation: Ranjit Singh issued few general commands, yet society was ordered by custom, so the command model overlooks customary law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states the opposite of what the example is used to show. Option C federalism, not this example, is used against indivisibility. Option D misreads the example: the ruler was obeyed, and the point concerns law-making.
questions.clat_trap: The example involves a despot, tempting candidates to read it as a point about obedience or power.
questions.language_trick: 'few general commands' while 'custom governed daily life'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): On Austin's account, custom by itself is law even if no court has ever applied it. Reason (R): Austin treated a custom adopted by the courts as a tacit command of the sovereign.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because for Austin custom becomes law only when courts adopt it. R is true and is the very reason A fails.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats A as true, though Austin made custom law only on adoption by the courts. Option B treats A as true, though Austin made custom law only on adoption by the courts. Option C treats A as true and R as false, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: R is an accurate statement that sounds like support for A, but it shows that adoption by courts is the condition.
questions.language_trick: 'by itself' and 'even if no court has ever applied it'.

questions.question: Hart's gunman illustration is meant to show that Austin's model

options.A: makes sovereignty divisible between several law-making bodies in a federal system
options.B: cannot distinguish being obliged to act from having an obligation to act
options.C: confuses positive morality with divine law in classifying rules
options.D: treats custom as law without any adoption by the courts

questions.explanation: A gunman orders and threatens; the victim is obliged, but has no obligation in the legal sense, which a command-and-threat model cannot mark.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the federalism objection, not the gunman point. Option C plays no part in the gunman illustration. Option D concerns the difference between coercion and obligation, not custom.
questions.clat_trap: Several objections to Austin are listed in the passage and candidates attach the wrong one to the illustration.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Austin's sovereign must itself be in the habit of obeying a superior. 2. Austin regarded a command as combining a wish, a sanction and a duty. 3. An Austinian sovereign is legally illimitable. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 restate the passage. Statement 1 reverses Austin's definition of the sovereign.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement 1, which reverses the definition of the sovereign as one not in a habit of obedience to a like superior. Option B includes statement 1 and omits statement 2. Option D includes statement 1, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: The negative in the definition ('not in a habit of obedience') is dropped in statement 1.
questions.language_trick: 'must itself be in the habit of obeying' against 'not in a habit of obedience'.

passages.subject_area: Jurisprudence (Pure Theory of Law and Judgments)
passages.title: Kelsen's Pure Theory and the Courts of Revolution
passages.passage: Hans Kelsen's Pure Theory of Law set out to describe 'what and how the law is', purged of politics, ethics, sociology and psychology. A legal norm is an 'ought' (Sollen) and is valid because it derives from a higher norm that authorises its creation. The legal order is therefore a hierarchy: individual judicial decisions rest on statutes, statutes on the constitution, and the historically first constitution on a presupposed basic norm, the Grundnorm, which is not enacted but presupposed, namely that one ought to behave as the framers of the first constitution have commanded. Kelsen separated validity from efficacy: a norm is valid not because it is obeyed, but because it belongs to a system which is, by and large, effective; the efficacy of the system as a whole is a condition, not the ground, of the validity of each norm. When a revolution or coup succeeds, the old Grundnorm is replaced, and the new order is valid because it has become effective. The Pakistan Supreme Court applied this reasoning in State v. Dosso (1958), holding that the abrogation of the 1956 Constitution was a successful revolution that created a new legal order. The High Court of Uganda, in Uganda v. Commissioner of Prisons, ex parte Matovu (1966), likewise treated a change of constitution as effective. In Asma Jilani v. Government of Punjab (1972), the Pakistan Supreme Court held Dosso wrongly decided: Kelsen's theory was no part of municipal law, efficacy alone could not validate the order of a usurper, and the Grundnorm of Pakistan lay in the legal and cultural aspirations of its people. The Privy Council, in Madzimbamuto v. Lardner-Burke (1968), refused to treat the 1965 Rhodesian regime as lawful, since the United Kingdom Parliament had retained legal sovereignty over Rhodesia.

questions.question: In the passage, the Grundnorm is best described as

options.A: the moral principle that law ought to be obeyed because it is just and reasonable
options.B: the first article of the written constitution, as enacted by its framers
options.C: the habit of obedience of the bulk of society to a determinate sovereign
options.D: a presupposed, not enacted, norm that validates the first historical constitution

questions.explanation: The Grundnorm is the presupposed basic norm that stands behind the first constitution and validates the whole hierarchy.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A imports morality, which the Pure Theory excludes. Option B makes it an enacted provision, whereas it is presupposed. Option C describes Austin's test of sovereignty, not Kelsen's basic norm.
questions.clat_trap: Austin's habit of obedience is a familiar competing idea and sits in a distractor.

questions.question: A statute is widely flouted in one district, but the legal system as a whole remains by and large effective. On Kelsen's view as described, the statute is

options.A: invalid, because a norm is valid only if it is morally justified to those bound
options.B: invalid, because the efficacy of each individual norm is the ground of its validity
options.C: still valid, since efficacy of the system as a whole is the condition of validity
options.D: valid only because it is flouted, since disobedience shows the exercise of power

questions.explanation: The passage says efficacy of the system as a whole is a condition, not the ground, of the validity of each norm.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A imports morality, which the Pure Theory excludes. Option B makes efficacy of each norm the ground of validity, contrary to the passage. Option D is a non sequitur found nowhere in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Efficacy is easily conflated with validity of each rule, which is the common mistake the passage warns against.
questions.language_trick: 'condition, not the ground' and 'system as a whole'.

questions.question: After a successful coup, soldiers suspend the constitution and the new regime governs effectively. Applying the reasoning in Dosso as described, the new order is

options.A: valid only if the former legislature ratifies it by resolution after the event
options.B: a valid legal order, since a successful revolution replaces the Grundnorm
options.C: invalid, since the old constitution remains valid until Parliament repeals it
options.D: valid only if it conforms to the legal and cultural aspirations of the people

questions.explanation: Dosso treated the abrogation as a successful revolution creating a new legal order valid because effective.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds a requirement that the Kelsenian thesis does not need. Option C ignores that a successful revolution displaces the old Grundnorm. Option D is the Asma Jilani test, not the Dosso reasoning.
questions.clat_trap: Jilani's test is placed in a distractor to catch candidates who merge the two decisions.

questions.question: Asma Jilani departs from Dosso mainly because the Court held that

options.A: Kelsen is no part of municipal law, and efficacy alone cannot validate a usurper
options.B: the 1956 Constitution had not in fact been abrogated by the military takeover
options.C: Austin's command theory supplies the correct test of legal validity in Pakistan
options.D: a revolution can never replace a Grundnorm in any circumstances whatever

questions.explanation: Jilani held Dosso wrongly decided: Kelsen is not part of municipal law, and efficacy alone cannot validate a usurper.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B the disagreement is about the legal effect of the change, not whether it occurred. Option C Austin is not invoked in the passage as Jilani's test. Option D overstates the holding; Jilani denies that efficacy alone suffices and looks to the people's aspirations.
questions.clat_trap: The extreme 'never' in a distractor is attractive to candidates who recall only that Jilani 'rejected' Dosso.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Matovu treated a change of constitution as effective. 2. In Madzimbamuto, the Privy Council treated the 1965 Rhodesian regime as a lawful revolution creating a new Grundnorm. 3. Dosso treated the abrogation of the 1956 Constitution as a successful revolution. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 and 3 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Matovu and Dosso applied the revolution reasoning; the Privy Council in Madzimbamuto refused to treat the Rhodesian regime as lawful.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A omits statement 3, which the passage states. Option B includes statement 2, which reverses the Privy Council's refusal to treat the regime as lawful. Option D includes statement 2, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: Three cases in one passage invite candidates to lump them together as Kelsenian.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Kelsen's Grundnorm is presupposed and not enacted. Reason (R): In Dosso, the Pakistan Supreme Court treated the abrogation of the 1956 Constitution as a successful revolution.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are in the passage, but Dosso's reasoning does not explain why the Grundnorm is presupposed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats R as the explanation of A, though a court's treatment of a coup does not explain what a Grundnorm is. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Two true statements from the same passage are paired so that candidates assume a causal link.
questions.language_trick: Test whether R explains A, not merely whether R is true.

passages.title: Rules, Principles and Discretion: Hart, Dworkin and Raz
passages.passage: H.L.A. Hart's The Concept of Law (1961) described a legal system as the union of primary and secondary rules and located validity in a rule of recognition accepted by officials from an internal point of view. Hart accepted that language has an 'open texture': a rule such as 'no vehicles in the park' has a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of doubt, and in penumbral cases the judge exercises discretion and legislates interstitially. Ronald Dworkin attacked this picture in 'The Model of Rules'. Law, he argued, contains not only rules, which apply in an 'all-or-nothing' fashion, but also principles, which have a dimension of weight and cannot be identified by a pedigree test. In Riggs v. Palmer (1889), the New York Court of Appeals refused to let a grandson who had murdered his grandfather take under the will, though the statute of wills made no exception, saying that 'No one shall be permitted to profit by his own fraud, or to take advantage of his own wrong, or to found any claim upon his own iniquity, or to acquire property by his own crime.' For Dworkin this showed that judges are bound by principles as law and so have no strong discretion in hard cases; there is a right answer, which an ideal judge, Hercules, would find by constructing the best moral justification of the legal practice, a method he later called law as integrity and compared to writing a chain novel. Rights, in his phrase, are trumps over collective goals. In a Postscript Hart replied that a rule of recognition may incorporate moral criteria, a view called inclusive positivism. Joseph Raz defended exclusive positivism: law is identified by its social sources alone, whatever its merit (the sources thesis), and where the sources run out judges exercise discretion.

questions.question: A council bylaw bans 'vehicles' from a park. Officials disagree whether a motorised child's toy car is covered. On Hart's analysis, this is

options.A: a case in which the rule of recognition is absent
options.B: a penumbral case in which open texture leaves the judge a discretion
options.C: a core case in which the rule clearly applies
options.D: a case with no legal answer, so the bylaw is void for uncertainty

questions.explanation: A toy car lies in the penumbra of 'vehicle', where the settled core gives out and the judge must choose.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses doubt about meaning with the absence of any criterion of validity. Option C treats a doubtful case as a settled core instance. Option D open texture does not void a rule; it leaves discretion in penumbral cases.
questions.clat_trap: The park example is the standard illustration; the trap is to treat doubt as invalidity.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts rules and principles in Dworkin's account as described?

options.A: Principles are law only if a legislature has enacted them, like any other rule
options.B: A valid rule decides the case if its conditions are met, whereas principles have weight
options.C: Principles apply in an all-or-nothing fashion, whereas rules have a dimension of weight
options.D: Rules and principles are both identified solely by a pedigree test of origin

questions.explanation: Rules apply all-or-nothing; principles have weight and need no pedigree.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A makes enactment the test, which Dworkin denies for principles. Option C reverses the roles of rules and principles. Option D contradicts the statement that principles cannot be identified by a pedigree test.
questions.clat_trap: The reversal in option A is the commonest slip when the two properties are memorised separately.
questions.language_trick: 'all-or-nothing' belongs to rules; 'dimension of weight' belongs to principles.

questions.question: Riggs v. Palmer matters to Dworkin's argument because the court

options.A: applied the sources thesis, since the statute expressly excluded murderers from taking under a will
options.B: held the statute of wills void for ignoring morality, and so struck it down in part as invalid
options.C: exercised a strong discretion to create a new rule for a gap in the statute of wills, as Hart describes
options.D: relied on a legal principle outside the statute, so that law is wider than rules found by pedigree

questions.explanation: The court applied the principle that no one may profit from his own wrong, though the statute was silent; for Dworkin, principles are law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A the statute made no exception at all. Option B the court did not strike down the statute. Option C gives the Hartian description of the case that Dworkin rejects.
questions.clat_trap: The distractor reproduces the Hartian explanation (discretion), which is exactly what the case is used to attack.
questions.language_trick: 'made no exception' signals that the principle came from outside the statute's text.

questions.question: Inclusive positivism differs from Dworkin's theory because inclusive positivists hold that

options.A: judges never have discretion in any case
options.B: principles are law because they morally justify the practice, whatever officials accept
options.C: moral criteria are part of the law only where the social rule of recognition incorporates them
options.D: morality can never be relevant to legal validity

questions.explanation: Inclusive positivism keeps validity dependent on a social rule of recognition, which may itself incorporate moral tests.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Dworkin's right-answer thesis. Option B states Dworkin's constructive-interpretation view, not inclusive positivism. Option D is Raz's exclusive positivism.
questions.clat_trap: Three positions are in play (inclusive, exclusive, Dworkin), and each distractor belongs to one of the others.
questions.language_trick: 'only where the social rule of recognition incorporates them'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Raz's exclusive positivism denies that moral tests can form part of the criteria of legal validity. Reason (R): Raz holds that law is identified by its social sources alone.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: If law is identified by social sources alone, moral tests cannot be among the criteria of validity, so R explains A.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats R as unconnected, though R is the very reason for A. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Inclusive and exclusive positivism are easily swapped, so candidates doubt A.

questions.question: Dworkin's description of rights as 'trumps over collective goals' implies that

options.A: a judge may weigh a right against a collective goal as an equal consideration in each case
options.B: a collective goal such as general welfare cannot by itself justify overriding an individual right
options.C: a right exists only if a statute has enacted it, since rights are creatures of legislation
options.D: an individual right yields whenever the majority finds it inconvenient to respect

questions.explanation: A trump defeats ordinary considerations; collective goals cannot override the right merely by being valuable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A an equal consideration is not a trump. Option C rights may exist as principles without enactment in his account. Option D states the opposite of the trumps idea.
questions.clat_trap: Weighing language ('weight') used for principles is stretched to rights, tempting candidates to choose equal weighing.
questions.language_trick: 'trump' means it beats, not merely competes with, collective goals.

passages.title: Legal Realism: Holmes, Gray, Llewellyn, Cardozo and the Scandinavians
passages.passage: American Legal Realism was a loose movement rather than a school. Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. began The Common Law (1881) with the remark that 'The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience.' In The Path of the Law (1897) he wrote: 'The prophecies of what the courts will do in fact, and nothing more pretentious, are what I mean by the law.' He asked lawyers to view law as a 'bad man' does, one who 'cares only for the material consequences' of his acts and not as a good man guided by conscience. John Chipman Gray, in The Nature and Sources of the Law (1909), said that statutes are sources of law, not law itself, because the law consists of the rules which the courts lay down. Karl Llewellyn wrote in The Bramble Bush (1930): 'What these officials do about disputes is, to my mind, the law itself.' His rule skepticism doubted that rules alone determine decisions, and he distinguished paper rules from real rules. Benjamin Cardozo, in The Nature of the Judicial Process (1921), identified four methods of adjudication: the method of philosophy (logical progression), the method of evolution (historical development), the method of tradition (custom) and the method of sociology (social welfare); he wrote that 'The final cause of law is the welfare of society.' Scandinavian realism, associated with Hagerstrom, Lundstedt, Olivecrona and Alf Ross, was psychological rather than behavioural. It denied that rights and duties correspond to any mystical power or metaphysical reality, treating them as words that guide conduct, and Ross treated valid law as the rules which courts actually apply because they feel them binding. Critics, notably Hart, argued that realists neglect the internal point of view of officials and cannot explain why rules matter to judges who apply them out of a sense of being bound.

questions.question: A client asks a lawyer only whether breaking a contract will cost him more than performing it. This approach most closely reflects Holmes's

options.A: method of philosophy, which follows logical progression
options.B: Scandinavian view that rights are mere words with no function
options.C: 'bad man' who cares only for the material consequences of his acts
options.D: good man guided by the vaguer sanctions of conscience

questions.explanation: The bad man wants to predict the material consequences of his conduct, so he asks what the courts will do in fact.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is a Cardozo method of adjudication, not Holmes's view of the client. Option B is a different school with a different claim. Option D describes the person Holmes contrasts with the bad man.
questions.clat_trap: Cardozo's and the Scandinavian ideas are offered in distractors because all are part of the 'realist' bundle.

questions.question: Gray's statement that statutes are sources of law and not law itself implies that a statute becomes law

options.A: only if its content conforms to the moral rights of the people
options.B: only through the rules the courts lay down in interpreting and applying it
options.C: only after it has been adopted as a custom by the community
options.D: the moment the legislature enacts it, whether or not a court ever applies it

questions.explanation: For Gray the law is what the courts lay down; statutes are materials from which courts draw it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A introduces a moral test unrelated to Gray's reasoning. Option C confuses statutes with custom as a source. Option D states the view Gray denies.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates assume legislation must be the paradigm of law and read the statement as a slogan.

questions.question: A judge faces a gap and resolves it by following the long-established usages of the trade concerned. Which of Cardozo's methods is this?

options.A: the method of tradition
options.B: the method of sociology
options.C: the method of evolution
options.D: the method of philosophy

questions.explanation: Reliance on established usage is the method of tradition, the third method in the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B seeks the social welfare outcome. Option C traces the historical development of the rule. Option D follows logical progression of a rule to its conclusion.
questions.clat_trap: Four similar-sounding methods are listed, and 'evolution' tempts because usages are historical.

questions.question: Scandinavian realism differs from American realism chiefly in that it

options.A: was grounded in natural law, treating rights as moral facts that exist independently of the courts
options.B: was sociological, treating law as social engineering that balances competing interests
options.C: was behavioural, defining law as predictions of what courts will do in fact
options.D: was psychological, denying metaphysical content to rights and treating law as rules felt binding on courts

questions.explanation: The passage calls Scandinavian realism psychological and anti-metaphysical, with Ross's emphasis on rules courts feel bound by.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the denial of any metaphysical reality for rights. Option B attributes Pound's idea to the Scandinavians. Option C describes Holmes's American approach, not the Scandinavian one.
questions.clat_trap: Both movements are called realist, so candidates assign the American predictive test to both.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Llewellyn's rule skepticism implies that rules play no role at all in judicial decisions. Reason (R): Llewellyn distinguished paper rules from real rules.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Rule skepticism doubts that rules alone determine outcomes; it does not deny every role to rules. R is correct.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats A as true, though skepticism doubted only that rules alone determine decisions. Option B treats A as true, though skepticism doubted only that rules alone determine decisions. Option C treats A as true and R as false, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: 'alone' is dropped in the assertion, turning a doubt into a denial.

questions.question: A judge applies a statute not from fear of reversal, but because he regards himself as bound by it. A pure prediction theory of law, according to Hart's criticism in the passage, fails here because it

options.A: ignores the four methods of adjudication identified by Cardozo in the judicial process
options.B: treats statutes as mere sources of law rather than as law, which is Gray's separate point
options.C: assumes that law is a command of a sovereign backed by threats, which is Austin's model
options.D: cannot capture the judge's internal acceptance of the rule as binding

questions.explanation: Hart's point is that realists neglect the internal point of view of officials who apply rules out of a sense of being bound.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A Cardozo's methods are not part of Hart's criticism. Option B is Gray's view, not Hart's criticism. Option C describes Austin's model, which is not the target here.
questions.clat_trap: Several named doctrines are available, and candidates attach the wrong critic to the wrong target.

passages.title: Salmond on Law and Justice; Will and Interest Theories of Rights
passages.passage: Sir John Salmond defined law as 'the body of principles recognised and applied by the State in the administration of justice', adding that law consists of the rules recognised and acted on by courts of justice. He defined the administration of justice as 'the maintenance of right within a political community by means of the physical force of the State', and divided it into civil and criminal justice: in civil justice the State enforces rights, while in criminal justice it punishes wrongs. Salmond defined a legal right as 'an interest recognised and protected by a rule of right', the violation of which is a legal wrong and respect for which is a legal duty. Every right has five elements: a subject (the owner), a person bound, a content (the act or forbearance required), an object (that in respect of which the right exists) and a title (the facts that vest the right in the owner). Two theories compete in explaining the nature of rights. The will theory, associated with Savigny and Windscheid, holds that a right is a sphere of power given by law to the will of the right-holder; it has difficulty with infants and persons of unsound mind, who have rights but no legal will. The interest theory, associated with Ihering and Bentham, holds that 'rights are legally protected interests'; critics reply that it cannot explain why the beneficiary of a contract to which he is not a party does not enjoy the right, and that criminal laws protect interests without conferring rights on each member of the public. Hart's choice theory refines the will theory by saying that a right-holder has control over the correlative duty. Salmond also divides rights into rights in rem, available against the world, and rights in personam, available against determinate persons; proprietary and personal rights; and perfect rights, enforceable by action, and imperfect rights, which are not, such as a debt barred by limitation.

questions.question: A lends B Rs 1,00,000 under a written loan agreement. In Salmond's analysis of A's right to repayment, the 'title' of the right is

options.A: the repayment of the money, which is the act or content required of B
options.B: the loan transaction, the fact that vests the right in A
options.C: A himself, who owns the right and is its subject
options.D: B, against whom the right is available as the person bound

questions.explanation: Title consists of the facts that vest the right in the owner; here, the loan agreement and payment of the money.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the content of the right, not its title. Option C is the subject or owner of the right. Option D is the person bound, not the title.
questions.clat_trap: All five elements are in play in one transaction, so any can be offered as 'the title'.

questions.question: Which of the following poses the greatest difficulty for the will theory of rights, according to the passage?

options.A: the rights of a beneficiary under a contract to which he is not a party
options.B: criminal laws that protect public interests without conferring individual rights
options.C: the rights of infants and persons of unsound mind, who have no legal will
options.D: the division of rights into rights in rem and in personam

questions.explanation: A will theory ties a right to the will of the holder, which infants and persons of unsound mind lack in law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the difficulty raised against the interest theory. Option B is also an objection to the interest theory. Option D is a classification and not an objection to the will theory.
questions.clat_trap: Objections to the two theories are listed side by side, so candidates attribute the wrong objection to the will theory.
questions.language_trick: 'no legal will' marks the will-theory problem.

questions.question: A and B contract that B will pay a sum to C, a stranger to the contract. C's interest is plainly protected, yet C cannot sue. This is cited against the

options.A: choice theory, since C has control over the duty and so ought to hold the right
options.B: the classification of rights as perfect or imperfect, since C's right is imperfect
options.C: will theory, since C has no will to exercise and so cannot hold a right
options.D: interest theory, since protecting C's interest does not give C the right

questions.explanation: The passage lists exactly this objection to the interest theory: the beneficiary's interest is protected yet he has no right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A C has no control over the duty, so the example does not count against the choice theory in this way. Option B that classification is not the subject of the objection. Option C the objection to the will theory concerns persons without legal will, not third-party beneficiaries.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates tend to apply the infant objection to every theory.
questions.language_trick: 'beneficiary of a contract to which he is not a party'.

questions.question: A debt which is barred by limitation, though morally owed, is in Salmond's classification

options.A: a right in rem, since it is available against the world
options.B: an imperfect right, since it is not enforceable by action
options.C: no right at all, since law protects no interest in it
options.D: a perfect right, since the debt still exists

questions.explanation: A time-barred debt is the passage's example of an imperfect right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A a debt is available against a determinate person, so it is in personam. Option C the passage treats it as an imperfect right, not no right. Option D perfect rights are enforceable by action.
questions.clat_trap: 'No right at all' is tempting because the creditor cannot sue.

questions.question: A religious body has detailed rules which its members observe strictly, but the courts of the State neither recognise nor apply them. On Salmond's definition of law, those rules are

options.A: not law, however strictly the members observe them
options.B: law, because they are principles of right for the members
options.C: law, because they are observed with greater regularity than many statutes
options.D: law, because they protect an interest that is a legal duty to respect

questions.explanation: On Salmond's definition law consists of principles recognised and applied by the State in the administration of justice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats morality as the test of law. Option C makes observance the test, whereas Salmond's test is recognition and application by the State's courts. Option D assumes legal recognition that the facts deny.
questions.clat_trap: Observance and morality are tempting tests, but the definition is institutional.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Rights in rem are available against determinate persons. 2. Salmond defined the administration of justice as the maintenance of right within a political community by means of the physical force of the State. 3. Ihering and Bentham are associated with the interest theory of rights. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1 and 2 only
options.C: 1 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 2 and 3 restate the passage; rights in rem are available against the world, not determinate persons.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B includes statement 1, which describes rights in personam. Option C relies on statement 1, which is false, and omits 2 and 3. Option D includes statement 1, which reverses rights in rem and in personam.
questions.clat_trap: In rem and in personam are swapped in statement 1.

passages.title: Legal Personality: Fiction, Concession and Realist Theories; Salomon and the Veil
passages.passage: A legal person is any entity to which the law attributes rights and duties. Natural persons are human beings; artificial or juristic persons include corporations, institutions and, in some systems, idols. Savigny's fiction theory holds that only human beings are real persons and that the law treats a corporation as a person by fiction; Salmond and Gray took a similar view. The concession theory says that a corporation exists because the State grants personality, which it can also withdraw. Gierke's realist or organic theory holds that groups are real social organisms with a will of their own, which the State merely recognises; Maitland, who translated Gierke, supported it. Brinz's bracket theory treats corporate assets as purposive property belonging to no one, and Ihering's symbolist theory sees the persons behind the corporation as the true beneficiaries. In Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd (1897), the House of Lords held that a company, once validly incorporated, is a separate entity. Lord Macnaghten said that 'the company is at law a different person altogether from the subscribers to the memorandum' and 'is not in law the agent of the subscribers or trustee for them'. Courts have nevertheless lifted the veil of incorporation where the company is a sham or a cloak for fraud. In Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne (1933), a company was formed to enable a former employee to solicit customers in breach of his covenant; in Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre Co. (1916), the court looked behind the company to determine enemy character. In Lee v. Lee's Air Farming Ltd (1961), the Privy Council held that a sole shareholder and director could also be an employee of his company. In India, Tata Engineering and Locomotive Co. v. State of Bihar (1964) recognised that the veil may be lifted, though the Court declined to do so there, and Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (1996) lifted the veil to reach the family-controlled companies of a fraudulent promoter.

questions.question: The theory that a group is a real social organism with a will of its own, which the State merely recognises, is

options.A: Gierke's realist or organic theory
options.B: Savigny's fiction theory of juristic personality
options.C: the concession theory of the State's grant of personality
options.D: Brinz's bracket theory of purposive property

questions.explanation: Gierke, followed by Maitland, held that groups are real organisms and the State only recognises them.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B holds that only human beings are real persons. Option C makes the State the source of personality. Option D treats corporate assets as purposive property of no one.
questions.clat_trap: Five theories of personality are in the passage, and candidates mismatch names and ideas.
questions.language_trick: 'real' and 'recognises' point to the realist theory.

questions.question: On the concession theory, as described, the State

options.A: must recognise every group as a person, since groups are real organisms
options.B: treats the corporation as a person only by a convenient fiction about its members
options.C: can never dissolve a corporation once it is incorporated
options.D: may withdraw the personality of a corporation, because it was granted by the State

questions.explanation: The concession theory makes the State the source of personality, so it can be withdrawn.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the realist theory. Option B is the fiction theory. Option C contradicts the idea that the State can withdraw what it granted.
questions.clat_trap: Fiction and concession theories are close; each distractor belongs to a different theory.

questions.question: A trader bound by a covenant not to solicit his former employer's customers forms a company, controlled by him, to solicit them. On the passage, a court may

options.A: refuse relief, because a sole shareholder may in law be an employee of his company
options.B: treat the company as a cloak and lift the veil to enforce the covenant against him
options.C: respect the separate personality of the company absolutely, since Salomon forbids lifting the veil
options.D: hold the company the agent of the trader's former employer

questions.explanation: Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne is the passage's example of a company formed to evade a covenant.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies Lee's Air Farming, which concerns employment status, not evasion of covenants. Option C ignores the passage's statement that courts lift the veil for sham or fraud. Option D invents an agency relationship found nowhere in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Lee's Air Farming is placed next to Gilford in the passage to tempt the wrong rationale.

questions.question: According to Lord Macnaghten's statement in Salomon as quoted, a company's relationship to its subscribers is that it

options.A: is a sham, since the business is precisely as before incorporation
options.B: is a separate person, and is neither their agent nor their trustee
options.C: is their agent, because the same persons manage it and take the profits
options.D: is their trustee, because the profits are received by them

questions.explanation: Macnaghten says the company is at law a different person and not the agent or trustee of the subscribers, even if the business is unchanged.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A the quoted words accept that the business may be the same and still hold the company separate. Option C is the proposition Macnaghten rejects in the quoted words. Option D is rejected in the quoted words.
questions.clat_trap: Plain commercial sense suggests the company is the members' agent, which is the error the passage warns against.
questions.language_trick: 'not in law the agent' is the operative phrase.

questions.question: Which Indian decision in the passage lifted the veil to reach the family-controlled companies of a fraudulent promoter?

options.A: Lee v. Lee's Air Farming Ltd (1961)
options.B: Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre Co. (1916)
options.C: Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (1996)
options.D: Tata Engineering and Locomotive Co. v. State of Bihar (1964)

questions.explanation: The passage says Skipper Construction lifted the veil; Tata Engineering recognised the power but declined to use it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is a Privy Council decision on a one-man company, not an Indian veil-lifting case. Option B is an English decision on enemy character. Option D recognised that the veil may be lifted but declined to do so in that case.
questions.clat_trap: Tata Engineering is the best known Indian name, so it draws candidates who ignore 'declined to do so there'.
questions.language_trick: 'declined to do so' versus 'lifted the veil'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A sole shareholder and director of a company may in law be an employee of that company. Reason (R): In Lee v. Lee's Air Farming Ltd, the Privy Council applied the separate personality of the company to hold that such a person could be an employee.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Lee is the authority for A and applies the separate-personality principle, so R explains A.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats R as unconnected, though R is the decision that supports A. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates fear that a one-man company is a sham, forgetting that separate personality is respected.
questions.language_trick: 'applied the separate personality' links R to A.

passages.title: Idols, Scriptures, Rivers and Animals: Juristic Personality in Indian Courts
passages.passage: Indian courts have extended juristic personality beyond human beings and companies. In Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925), the Privy Council held that a Hindu idol is a juristic entity with the power of suing and being sued, acting through a shebait, who is its human representative and manager; the dedicated property vests in the idol and not in the shebait. In Yogendra Nath Naskar v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1969), the Supreme Court held that a deity can be assessed to income tax as an 'individual'. In Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee v. Som Nath Dass (2000), the Court held that the Guru Granth Sahib is a juristic person, reasoning by analogy with the idol in Hindu law. In the Ayodhya judgment, M. Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das (2019), the Court recognised the deity, Ram Lalla Virajman, as a juristic person who may sue through a next friend. In Mohd. Salim v. State of Uttarakhand (2017), the Uttarakhand High Court declared the rivers Ganga and Yamuna to be legal persons with the rights, duties and liabilities of a living person, and named officials as persons in loco parentis to protect them, following New Zealand's Te Awa Tupua Act 2017, which gave legal personality to the Whanganui River. The Supreme Court stayed that order on the State's appeal. In Karnail Singh v. State of Haryana (2019), the Punjab and Haryana High Court declared the entire animal kingdom to be legal entities with a distinct persona, with citizens as persons in loco parentis. The Supreme Court's own approach to animals is more cautious. In Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (2014), it held that animals have statutory rights under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 and that duties of compassion arise under Article 51A(g), and it said that these rights should be elevated to the status of fundamental rights, but it did not declare animals legal persons.

questions.question: Under the position in Pramatha Nath Mullick, property dedicated to an idol vests in

options.A: the shebait, who holds it as owner for the worshippers
options.B: the worshippers of the idol in equal shares
options.C: the State, which acts as trustee of religious endowments
options.D: the idol itself, with the shebait acting as its manager

questions.explanation: The idol is the juristic owner; the shebait is only its representative and manager.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the rule that the property vests in the idol and not in the shebait. Option B has no support in the passage. Option C has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates mix up the owner with the manager, since the shebait controls the property in practice.
questions.language_trick: 'vests in the idol and not in the shebait'.

questions.question: A temple deity owns agricultural land and earns rent. Under Yogendra Nath Naskar as described, the rental income is assessable

options.A: in the hands of the deity as an 'individual', represented by the shebait
options.B: in no one's hands, since religious property is outside the tax system
options.C: in the hands of the shebait personally, since the deity cannot own property
options.D: in the hands of each worshipper in proportion to his devotion

questions.explanation: The Court held that the deity may be assessed to income tax as an individual.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B has no basis in the passage, which treats the deity as assessable. Option C contradicts the idol's juristic personality and ownership. Option D has no basis in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates assume personality is only for suits, not tax, forgetting that it carries liabilities as well as rights.
questions.language_trick: 'individual' in the Income Tax Act includes the deity.

questions.question: In Som Nath Dass, the Court's reasoning that the Guru Granth Sahib is a juristic person proceeded by

options.A: holding that the Gurdwara Committee itself owns the scripture
options.B: analogy with the idol in Hindu law
options.C: reliance on the Te Awa Tupua Act 2017
options.D: analogy with the corporate personality of companies under Salomon

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court reasoned by analogy with the idol in Hindu law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the finding that the scripture is itself the juristic person. Option C postdates the decision by many years. Option D is not the reasoning described in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The 2017 river decisions are later and cannot be a basis for a 2000 decision.

questions.question: The Uttarakhand High Court's order declaring the Ganga and Yamuna to be legal persons was

options.A: inspired by the New Zealand statute on the Whanganui River and stayed by the Supreme Court
options.B: based on Pramatha Nath Mullick, with each river treated as a deity in the Hindu law sense
options.C: affirmed by a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court as the settled law of the land
options.D: founded on the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, extended to rivers and other natural features

questions.explanation: The High Court followed Te Awa Tupua Act 2017; the Supreme Court stayed the order on the State's appeal.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is not stated in the passage. Option C contradicts the stay. Option D that Act concerns animals, not rivers.
questions.clat_trap: 'Legal person' sounds like an established holding, so candidates assume affirmation.

questions.question: Which statement correctly states the Supreme Court's position in Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (2014) as described?

options.A: It held that animals have no rights at all, only duties of care owed to them by humans under Article 51A(g)
options.B: It declared animals to be legal persons with all the rights, duties and liabilities of a living person
options.C: It held that animals' rights arise only under Article 51A(g) of the Constitution and not under any statute
options.D: It accepted statutory rights of animals and urged their elevation to fundamental rights, but not legal personality

questions.explanation: The Court accepted statutory rights and urged elevation to fundamental rights without declaring legal personality.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is inconsistent with its recognition of statutory rights. Option B is the High Court's approach in Karnail Singh, not the Supreme Court's. Option C ignores the rights under the 1960 Act.
questions.clat_trap: Karnail Singh and Nagaraja are both animal cases, so candidates attribute the bolder holding to the Supreme Court.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A deity's dedicated property vests in the shebait. Reason (R): The shebait is the human representative and manager of the deity.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because the property vests in the idol; R is true because the shebait is the representative and manager.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats A as true, though the property vests in the idol and not the shebait. Option B treats A as true, though the property vests in the idol and not the shebait. Option C treats A as true and R as false, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: R describes the shebait's control, which tempts candidates to credit him with ownership.

passages.title: Theories of Property and Ownership: Locke, Bentham, Honore and the Public Trust
passages.passage: Locke's labour theory begins from a common earth: 'every man has a property in his own person ... The labour of his body and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his.' It carried two limits: enough and as good must be left for others, and nothing may be allowed to spoil. Bentham's utilitarian account denies any natural property: 'Property and law are born together, and die together. Before laws were made there was no property; take away laws, and property ceases.' Hegel saw property as the embodiment of personality, and Marx saw private ownership of the means of production as the root of class exploitation. Austin defined ownership as 'a right indefinite in point of user, unrestricted in point of disposition, and unlimited in point of duration, over a determinate thing'. Salmond stressed that the right of ownership is the residuary right, indefinite in duration, and comprising possession, enjoyment and disposition. A.M. Honore, in 1961, listed eleven standard incidents of full liberal ownership: the rights to possess, use, manage, the income and the capital, the right to security, transmissibility, absence of term, the prohibition of harmful use, liability to execution, and residuary character. He observed that a person may be an owner though some incidents are missing, so that ownership is a cluster and not an absolute. The public trust doctrine, traced to Justinian's Institutes and developed in Illinois Central Railroad v. Illinois (1892), holds that certain resources, such as the seashore, running waters, air and forests, are held by the State not as owner but as trustee for the public. The Supreme Court applied it in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997), where the State had leased forest land on the bank of the Beas river to a private motel; the Court held the doctrine to be part of Indian law, quashed the lease and imposed costs for restoring the damage.

questions.question: Which of the following is a limit on appropriation in Locke's labour theory, as stated in the passage?

options.A: the sovereign must grant a licence for the appropriation
options.B: the appropriator must pay the community a rent for the thing
options.C: the appropriator must have the consent of every other person
options.D: enough and as good must be left for others

questions.explanation: Locke's two limits are the sufficiency proviso and the non-spoilage proviso.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds a state-grant requirement absent from Locke's account. Option B is not among the stated limits. Option C is a consent condition not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates import the social-contract idea of consent into a theory based on labour.

questions.question: A claimant says that his property in a piece of land exists by nature and would continue even if every law were repealed. A follower of Bentham, as presented in the passage, would answer that

options.A: property arises from mixing labour with an unowned thing, whatever the law says
options.B: property is the embodiment of the owner's personality
options.C: property is created by law, so that if laws are taken away property ceases
options.D: property is valid only if it is the root of class exploitation

questions.explanation: Bentham holds that property and law are born together and die together.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states Locke's theory, not Bentham's. Option B is Hegel's view. Option D garbles Marx's critique into a test of validity.
questions.clat_trap: Locke, Hegel and Marx are all in the passage, and each distractor belongs to one of them.

questions.question: A holds land for his life only, with no power to pass it beyond his death. Of Honore's incidents, the one that A lacks is

options.A: the right to use
options.B: the prohibition of harmful use
options.C: the right to possess
options.D: absence of term

questions.explanation: A life interest has a term, so the incident of absence of term is missing, though he may still be called an owner in a loose sense on Honore's cluster view.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A A may use the land during his life. Option B applies to every owner and is not something A lacks. Option C A has possession during his life.
questions.clat_trap: A life tenant has so many incidents that candidates struggle to isolate the one that is missing.

questions.question: Honore's list differs from Austin's definition of ownership in that Honore

options.A: treats ownership as a cluster of incidents present in varying degree, not one unlimited right
options.B: denies that an owner may possess the thing owned, treating possession as a separate matter
options.C: treats ownership as a right unlimited in duration and unrestricted in disposition
options.D: holds that ownership exists only where all eleven incidents are present together

questions.explanation: Honore observed that an owner may lack some incidents, so ownership is a cluster, whereas Austin defined it as an unlimited right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B contradicts the listing of possession as the first incident. Option C restates Austin's definition. Option D contradicts the observation that an owner may lack some incidents.
questions.clat_trap: Option A restates Austin and catches candidates who have not compared the two definitions.

questions.question: A State leases forest land on a riverbank to a private company for a resort. On M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath as described, the lease is

options.A: liable to be quashed, since the State holds such resources as trustee for the public
options.B: valid, provided the rent paid to the State is adequate and the lessee is a responsible company
options.C: valid, provided the company pays costs for any damage that it later causes to the area
options.D: valid, because the State as owner may lease its land to anyone on terms it chooses

questions.explanation: Kamal Nath applied the public trust doctrine and quashed a lease of riverbank forest land to a motel.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B makes the price the test, which the doctrine does not. Option C treats compensation as a substitute for the trust. Option D ignores the public trust doctrine.
questions.clat_trap: The State's ordinary power to lease its land is a common-sense answer that the doctrine overrides.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Salmond described the right of ownership as the residuary right, indefinite in duration. 2.
