Honore held that a person is an owner only if every one of the eleven incidents is present. 3. The public trust doctrine treats the State as trustee, not owner, of certain natural resources. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 1, 2 and 3
options.D: 1 and 3 only

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 restate the passage; Honore allowed that an owner may lack some incidents.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement 2, which contradicts Honore's cluster view. Option B omits statement 3, which is correct. Option C includes statement 2, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: 'every one' and 'only if' convert Honore's flexible list into a rigid test.
questions.language_trick: 'only if every one' against 'though some incidents are missing'.

passages.title: Judicial Precedent: Ratio, Obiter, Per Incuriam and Overruling
passages.passage: Under the doctrine of stare decisis, a court follows earlier decisions of courts above it and, in some systems, its own. The binding part of a decision is its ratio decidendi, the principle of law necessary for the decision on the material facts; observations beyond it are obiter dicta, which are persuasive only. Lord Halsbury said in Quinn v. Leathem (1901) that every judgment must be read as applicable to the particular facts proved, since the generality of its expressions is not intended to expound the whole law, and that 'a case is only an authority for what it actually decides'. In State of Orissa v. Sudhansu Sekhar Misra (1968), the Supreme Court repeated that a decision is an authority for what it actually decides, and not for what may logically be deduced from its observations. Article 141 of the Constitution provides that 'the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India'. A decision given per incuriam, in ignorance of a binding statute or authority, does not bind. In England, Young v. Bristol Aeroplane Co. (1944) held that the Court of Appeal is bound by its own decisions, subject to three exceptions: conflicting decisions, a decision inconsistent with a House of Lords decision, and a decision per incuriam. By the Practice Statement of 1966, the House of Lords gave itself liberty to depart from its own decisions 'when it appears right to do so'. The Indian Supreme Court is not bound by its own earlier decisions. Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar (1955) held that Article 141 does not prevent it from reconsidering them, and Keshav Mills Co. v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1965) added that reconsideration should be exercised sparingly and only for substantial and compelling reasons. Within the Court, a Bench cannot disagree with the decision of a coordinate or larger Bench; it may refer the question to a larger Bench, as laid down in Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v. State of Maharashtra (1998). Prospective overruling, introduced in India in I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), allows a court to overrule an earlier decision while applying the new rule only to future cases.

questions.question: A High Court is told that a passing remark in an earlier Supreme Court judgment, on a point not necessary for the decision, supports one party. On the passage, the remark is

options.A: without any value, since only the ratio of a judgment can ever be cited in court
options.B: binding on the High Court under Article 141, since the Court spoke it
options.C: obiter dictum, which is persuasive but not the binding ratio under Article 141
options.D: binding if it logically follows from the Court's other observations

questions.explanation: Only the ratio binds; obiter dicta are persuasive.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A obiter is persuasive, not valueless. Option B treats every observation as law declared, which Sudhansu Sekhar Misra rejects. Option D makes logical deduction a source of binding force, contrary to the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The grandeur of the Supreme Court tempts candidates to treat everything it says as binding.

questions.question: A Court of Appeal panel finds that its own earlier decision was rendered in ignorance of a relevant binding statute. Under Young v. Bristol Aeroplane as described, the panel

options.A: may depart because it prefers a different view of the law
options.B: is not bound by that decision, since it was given per incuriam
options.C: may depart only if the House of Lords uses the 1966 Practice Statement
options.D: is bound, because the Court of Appeal is bound by all its own decisions without exception

questions.explanation: Per incuriam is one of the three recognised exceptions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A mere preference is not one of the exceptions. Option C confuses the House of Lords's liberty with the Court of Appeal's exceptions. Option D ignores the three exceptions.
questions.clat_trap: The 1966 Practice Statement, a different court's rule, is placed in a distractor.
questions.language_trick: 'in ignorance of a binding statute' defines per incuriam.

questions.question: Taken together, Bengal Immunity and Keshav Mills mean that the Indian Supreme Court

options.A: may depart from earlier decisions freely, whenever a Bench disagrees with them
options.B: may reconsider its earlier decisions, but sparingly and only for compelling reasons
options.C: is absolutely bound by its earlier decisions under Article 141 of the Constitution
options.D: may depart from earlier decisions only with the approval of Parliament by legislation

questions.explanation: Bengal Immunity allows reconsideration; Keshav Mills restricts it to substantial and compelling reasons.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the Keshav Mills restraint. Option C Bengal Immunity held otherwise. Option D has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Two cases push in opposite directions, and candidates remember only one.

questions.question: A three-judge Bench of the Supreme Court doubts the correctness of a five-judge Bench decision. Under Dawoodi Bohra as described, the proper course is to

options.A: overrule the five-judge decision, as the later Bench is better informed
options.B: refer the question to a larger Bench
options.C: decline to decide the case until Parliament legislates
options.D: hold the earlier decision per incuriam and ignore it

questions.explanation: A Bench cannot disagree with a larger Bench, but it may refer the question to a larger Bench.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A a smaller Bench cannot overrule a larger one. Option C has no support in the passage. Option D is not available merely because the Bench doubts the decision.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates think a later decision always prevails.

questions.question: A court overrules an earlier precedent, but directs that the new rule applies only to transactions occurring after the date of its judgment. This is

options.A: retrospective overruling, applied to all past transactions
options.B: distinguishing the precedent on its facts
options.C: prospective overruling, introduced in India in I.C. Golaknath
options.D: reading down the precedent as obiter

questions.explanation: The passage defines prospective overruling as overruling with the new rule applying to future cases.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the opposite. Option B leaves the precedent standing, which overruling does not. Option D does not overrule it.
questions.clat_trap: Overruling, distinguishing and treating as obiter are three ways of avoiding a precedent, easily confused.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Article 141 binds the Supreme Court to follow every one of its own earlier decisions. Reason (R): Article 141 provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: R states the text of Article 141, but A is false because the Court can reconsider its own decisions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats A as true, though Bengal Immunity held that Article 141 does not bind the Court to its own decisions. Option B treats A as true, though Bengal Immunity held that Article 141 does not bind the Court to its own decisions. Option C treats A as true and R as false, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: An accurate quotation is paired with an inaccurate consequence.
questions.language_trick: 'all courts' does not include the Supreme Court itself as to reconsideration, per Bengal Immunity.

passages.subject_area: Jurisprudence (Sources of Law: Custom and Legislation)
passages.title: Custom and Legislation as Sources of Law
passages.passage: Salmond distinguished formal sources, from which law derives its force as law, namely the will of the State, from material sources, from which it derives its matter. Material sources are legal, recognised by the law itself (legislation, precedent, custom and agreement), or historical, such as the writings of jurists. Blackstone's tests of a valid custom were that it must be immemorial, continued, peaceable, reasonable, certain, compulsory and consistent with other customs. In Hurpurshad v. Sheo Dayal (1876), the Privy Council said that special usages modifying the ordinary law must be ancient and invariable and proved by clear and unambiguous evidence, and in Collector of Madura v. Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868) it observed that 'under the Hindu system of law, clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law'. A custom that is immoral or opposed to public policy is not enforced. The Constitution recognises custom: Article 13(3)(a) provides that 'law' includes 'any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law', so a custom may be struck down if it infringes Part III. In State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali (1951), the Bombay High Court held that personal laws derived from scriptural sources were not 'laws in force' under Article 13, distinguishing them from custom; that distinction has been criticised and remains contested. Legislation, in Salmond's definition, is that source of law which consists in the declaration of legal rules by a competent authority. It may be supreme, if it cannot be repealed or annulled by any other authority, or subordinate. In India, delegation of legislative power is permitted, but essential legislative functions cannot be delegated, as the Court held in In re Delhi Laws Act (1951).

questions.question: Which of the following is a historical source rather than a legal source on Salmond's classification as described?

options.A: legislation enacted by a competent authority
options.B: the writings of learned jurists
options.C: custom having the force of law
options.D: precedent laid down by the courts

questions.explanation: The passage lists legislation, precedent, custom and agreement as legal sources, and jurists' writings as a historical source.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is a legal source, recognised by the law itself. Option C is a legal source. Option D is a legal source.
questions.clat_trap: Jurists' writings are cited in court, so candidates assume they are legal sources.
questions.language_trick: 'recognised by the law itself' is the test of a legal source.

questions.question: A village claims an ancient custom, supported only by recollections of a few elders about the last thirty years. On the passage, a court is likely to

options.A: accept it, provided the village elders are unanimous in their recollection
options.B: accept it, because the recollection of living persons is the best evidence of custom
options.C: accept it, because custom outweighs statute in every case without exception
options.D: reject the custom, as it is not shown by clear evidence to be ancient and invariable

questions.explanation: Hurpurshad requires usages to be ancient and invariable and proved by clear and unambiguous evidence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A unanimity of recollection does not supply antiquity. Option B ignores the requirement of antiquity and clear proof. Option C overstates; the passage speaks only of usage outweighing the written text under Hindu law.
questions.clat_trap: A recent, vivid custom feels authentic, so candidates accept it.

questions.question: Under Hindu law, a written text states one rule and a clearly proved usage states another. According to Collector of Madura,

options.A: the rule that is more reasonable prevails, whatever its source
options.B: neither prevails and the court must apply equity
options.C: the written text prevails, since texts are always older than usage
options.D: the proved usage prevails over the written text

questions.explanation: The Privy Council observed that clear proof of usage outweighs the written text under the Hindu system.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A makes reasonableness the sole test, which the quotation does not. Option B has no support in the passage. Option C contradicts the quoted observation.
questions.clat_trap: Common sense says texts prevail over unwritten practice.

questions.question: A custom having the force of law discriminates between persons on the ground of sex in a matter of public employment. On Article 13(3)(a) as quoted, the custom is

options.A: persuasive only, so that the court may merely recommend that it be changed by the community
options.B: outside Article 13, because only enacted rules made by a legislature are 'law'
options.C: valid, because customs are older than the Constitution and are saved by their antiquity
options.D: 'law' for Article 13 and may be struck down if it infringes Part III

questions.explanation: Article 13(3)(a) includes custom or usage having the force of law within 'law'.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A Article 13 gives power to strike down, not just to recommend. Option B ignores the express mention of custom or usage. Option C age does not exempt a custom from Part III.
questions.clat_trap: Custom is unwritten, so candidates treat it as outside constitutional review.
questions.language_trick: 'custom or usage having ... the force of law'.

questions.question: The distinction drawn in State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali is between

options.A: the classification of sources into formal sources, which give law its force, and material sources, which give it its matter
options.B: ancient customs, which are enforceable, and recent customs, which a court will not enforce unless proved ancient
options.C: custom or usage, which is 'law' under Article 13, and scriptural personal law, said not to be a 'law in force'
options.D: supreme legislation, which no other authority can repeal, and subordinate legislation, which rests on delegated power

questions.explanation: Narasu held that scriptural personal laws were not 'laws in force' under Article 13, distinguishing them from custom; the distinction is contested.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Salmond's classification, not Narasu's distinction. Option B is not the distinction drawn in the case. Option D is the classification of legislation, not the Narasu distinction.
questions.clat_trap: Several classifications appear in the passage, and the 'distinction' language invites a mismatch.
questions.language_trick: 'law in force' is the key phrase.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Salmond treated the will of the State as the formal source of law. 2. Essential legislative functions cannot be delegated, as held in In re Delhi Laws Act. 3. Collector of Madura held that a written text of Hindu law always prevails over a proved usage. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 3 only
options.B: 1, 2 and 3
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1 and 2 only

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 restate the passage; statement 3 reverses Collector of Madura.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contains only statement 3, which reverses the Privy Council's observation. Option B includes statement 3, which is false. Option C includes statement 3 and omits statement 1.
questions.clat_trap: 'always prevails' reverses 'clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text'.
questions.language_trick: 'always' is the extreme word that flags the false statement.

passages.title: Theories of Punishment and the Indian Sentencing Cases
passages.passage: Theories of punishment are commonly classed as retributive, deterrent, preventive, reformative and expiatory. Retributive theory, associated with Kant and Hegel, holds that the offender deserves punishment because he has done wrong and that the punishment should be proportionate to the wrong; for Kant, punishing a person merely to deter others uses him as a means and violates the categorical imperative. Bentham, a utilitarian, held that 'all punishment in itself is evil' and is justified only 'in as far as it promises to exclude some greater evil'. Salmond wrote that 'Punishment is before all things deterrent', though retribution has a secondary place. Preventive theory aims at disabling the offender, reformative theory at rehabilitating him, and Durkheim linked punishment to reaffirmation of the collective conscience. Hart separated the general justifying aim of punishment from the questions of who may be punished and how much, arguing that retributive principles limit who may be punished and how much, while the justifying aim may be utilitarian. In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980), a Constitution Bench upheld the death penalty but confined it to the 'rarest of rare' cases, requiring courts to weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances; Machhi Singh (1983) later listed categories for guidance. In Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983), section 303 of the Indian Penal Code, which made death mandatory for a murder committed by a life convict, was struck down as violating Articles 14 and 21. In Mohd. Giasuddin v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1977), Krishna Iyer J. stressed the reformative purpose of sentencing. In Swamy Shraddananda (2008), the Court devised a sentence of life imprisonment for a fixed term beyond fourteen years, or for the whole of life without remission, as an alternative to death; the Constitution Bench in V. Sriharan (2015) upheld such sentences but held that only the High Courts and the Supreme Court may impose them. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 adds community service as a punishment in section 4, which it prescribes for petty offences such as the theft of property worth less than five thousand rupees by a first offender who restores it.

questions.question: Kant's objection to punishing an offender merely in order to deter others is that it

options.A: uses the offender as a means and so violates the categorical imperative
options.B: fails to reaffirm the collective conscience of the society in which it is imposed
options.C: treats punishment as an evil that exceeds the harm that it prevents in the future
options.D: makes the offender's rehabilitation secondary to the aim of deterrence

questions.explanation: For Kant punishment must rest on desert; deterrence alone uses the person merely as a means.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is Durkheim's idea. Option C is Bentham's utilitarian calculation, not Kant's objection. Option D is the reformative objection, not Kant's.
questions.clat_trap: Four theorists and four rationales are in the passage, and each distractor belongs to another.
questions.language_trick: 'as a means' is the Kantian phrase.

questions.question: According to Hart's position as described, retributive principles in a system of punishment serve to

options.A: limit who may be punished and how much, while the justifying aim may be utilitarian
options.B: justify punishment solely by its tendency to prevent crime in the future
options.C: supply the general justifying aim, making desert the only purpose of punishment
options.D: replace the need for proportionality in sentencing and for limits on liability

questions.explanation: Hart separates the justifying aim from the distribution of punishment; retributive principles govern the latter.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is the utilitarian aim, not retributive principle. Option C ignores the separation of aim and distribution. Option D contradicts the limiting function.
questions.clat_trap: Hart's view is a hybrid, and candidates choose one pure theory.
questions.language_trick: 'limit who may be punished and how much'.

questions.question: A statute provides that a person already serving a life sentence shall be sentenced to death, without discretion, if convicted of murder. On Mithu v. State of Punjab as described, such a provision is

options.A: valid, if the Governor may later commute the sentence
options.B: unconstitutional, as it violates Articles 14 and 21
options.C: valid, because sentencing policy is for the legislature alone
options.D: valid, since Bachan Singh upheld the death penalty

questions.explanation: Section 303, which made death mandatory for such a convict, was struck down under Articles 14 and 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A executive clemency cannot cure a mandatory sentence. Option C ignores the constitutional challenge upheld in Mithu. Option D Bachan Singh requires weighing of circumstances, which a mandatory sentence excludes.
questions.clat_trap: Bachan Singh and Mithu are both death penalty cases, and candidates assume the first validates the second.

questions.question: A sessions court wishes to impose life imprisonment for a fixed term of thirty years without remission. Under V. Sriharan as described, the court

options.A: may do so if the State Government approves the sentence in advance of the trial
options.B: may do so, since Swamy Shraddananda permits every court to impose such a sentence
options.C: may do so if the accused consents to the imposition of such a sentence
options.D: cannot do so, since only the High Courts and the Supreme Court may impose such sentences

questions.explanation: Sriharan upheld Swamy Shraddananda sentences but confined their imposition to the High Courts and the Supreme Court.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A executive approval is not the test. Option B overlooks the restriction in Sriharan. Option C consent is not the test.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates remember that such sentences exist but forget the limit on who may impose them.
questions.language_trick: 'only the High Courts and the Supreme Court'.

questions.question: A first offender convicted of theft of a mobile phone worth Rs 4,000 restores the phone to the owner. On the passage's reference to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the prescribed punishment is

options.A: forfeiture of the offender's property
options.B: fine only, with no other form of punishment
options.C: community service
options.D: rigorous imprisonment for not less than one year

questions.explanation: Section 4 includes community service, prescribed for petty theft below five thousand rupees by a first offender who restores the property.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A has no connection to the petty theft provision described. Option B is not the form of punishment the passage describes for this case. Option D is not the prescribed punishment for a first-time petty offender who restores the property.
questions.clat_trap: Facts must be matched to three conditions: value, first offence and restoration.
questions.language_trick: 'less than five thousand rupees' and 'first offender'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Supreme Court in Mithu v. State of Punjab struck down section 303 of the Indian Penal Code. Reason (R): In Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court confined the death penalty to the rarest of rare cases.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but R states a different decision and does not explain why section 303 fell.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats R as the explanation of A, though Bachan Singh was a different decision and did not itself strike down section 303. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Two death-penalty decisions are paired to suggest a causal link.
questions.language_trick: Test whether R explains A, not merely whether R is true.

passages.title: Legal Fictions: Maine, Bentham, Asquith and Indian Practice
passages.passage: A legal fiction is an assumption that something is true although it is known to be false, or a statutory deeming, adopted to reach a legal result. Sir Henry Maine used the word in a wide sense in Ancient Law: 'any assumption which conceals, or affects to conceal, the fact that a rule of law has undergone alteration, its letter remaining unchanged, its operation being modified.' He named fictions, equity and legislation as the three agencies by which law is brought into harmony with society, and regarded fictions as most useful in the early stages of legal development. Bentham condemned them: 'In English law, fiction is a wilful falsehood, having for its object the stealing of legislative power', by hands that could not or dared not claim it openly. Examples include the adoption of a child as born into the adoptive family, the personality of a corporation, and constructive notice. In East End Dwellings Co. Ltd v. Finsbury Borough Council (1952), Asquith LJ said: 'If you are bidden to treat an imaginary state of affairs as real, you must surely, unless prohibited from doing so, also imagine as real the consequences and incidents which, if the putative state of affairs had in fact existed, must inevitably have flowed from or accompanied it.' Indian courts adopt this reasoning but add that a fiction is confined to the purpose for which it was created: where a statute says that a person 'shall be deemed' to be something, the deeming operates for the stated purposes and is not extended beyond them. A fiction differs from a presumption, which can be rebutted by evidence, whereas a fiction cannot be disputed within its field, and from an estoppel, which depends on a representation made to the other party.

questions.question: A court holds that a parent is liable for an act of his child by assuming, contrary to fact, that the child was acting as the parent's agent, and thereby alters the old rule while its wording stays the same. In Maine's terms this is

options.A: a presumption, since it can be rebutted by the parent through contrary evidence
options.B: equity, since it applies principles of fairness from outside the strict law
options.C: legislation, since the court has openly changed the written rule of liability
options.D: a legal fiction, since it conceals the alteration behind an unchanged letter

questions.explanation: Maine's definition covers any assumption that conceals the alteration of a rule, its letter remaining unchanged.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A a presumption is a different concept and the facts do not suggest rebuttal. Option B the passage describes equity as a separate agency. Option C legislation alters the rule openly, whereas this conceals the alteration.
questions.clat_trap: The trap is to choose 'legislation' because the rule has plainly changed.

questions.question: A statute provides that a person appointed to a post 'shall be deemed to have been in service from 1 January'. Nothing in the statute forbids it. On Asquith LJ's dictum, he is

options.A: entitled to everything he claims, even benefits that the fiction was never meant to cover
options.B: not entitled to any consequence, since the deeming is a mere label with no effect
options.C: entitled to the consequences that would have flowed had he in fact been in service from that date
options.D: entitled only to the title and not to any related benefit that would have followed

questions.explanation: The dictum requires the consequences and incidents of the assumed state to be imagined as real, unless prohibited.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A extends the fiction beyond its purpose, which Indian courts forbid. Option B ignores the instruction to imagine the consequences as real. Option D stops short of the 'inevitably flowed' consequences.
questions.clat_trap: Option C goes too far, and Option A not far enough, so a middle path is the safest reading.

questions.question: A statute deems an unregistered society 'to be a firm' for the limited purpose of income tax. Can the society also be treated as a firm for the purposes of an unrelated criminal statute? On the passage,

options.A: no, since the deeming operates for the stated purpose and is not extended beyond it
options.B: no, since fictions can never apply to societies
options.C: yes, since once a fiction applies it operates for every purpose
options.D: yes, since Asquith LJ requires all consequences to be imagined without limit

questions.explanation: Indian courts confine a fiction to the purpose for which it was created.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B invents a limit not in the passage. Option C ignores the purpose limit. Option D ignores the limit that Indian courts add to the dictum.
questions.clat_trap: Asquith's dictum seems to be unlimited, but the passage adds the purpose limit.

questions.question: The principal difference between a legal fiction and a presumption, according to the passage, is that

options.A: a presumption can be rebutted by evidence, but a fiction cannot be disputed in its field
options.B: a presumption conceals an alteration of the rule of law behind an unchanged letter
options.C: a fiction depends on a representation made to the other party, who has acted on it
options.D: a fiction can be rebutted by evidence, whereas a presumption cannot be disputed

questions.explanation: A presumption is rebuttable; a fiction is not, within its field.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B describes Maine's fiction. Option C describes estoppel. Option D reverses the difference.
questions.clat_trap: Estoppel and fiction are also mentioned and are easily jumbled.

questions.question: Bentham's objection to fictions, as quoted in the passage, is chiefly that they

options.A: allow courts to adjust law to the needs of society through equity and fairness
options.B: conflict with the principle that consequences of an assumption must be imagined as real
options.C: are falsehoods that covertly take legislative power into hands that dare not claim it openly
options.D: are useful only in the early stages of legal development, and are later unnecessary

questions.explanation: Bentham called fiction a wilful falsehood whose object is the stealing of legislative power.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A describes Maine's view of equity as an agency of change. Option B is not Bentham's point and misuses Asquith's dictum. Option D is Maine's mild view, not Bentham's condemnation.
questions.clat_trap: Maine and Bentham treat the same device in opposite spirits, so candidates borrow Maine's praise.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Maine named fictions, equity and legislation as agencies by which law is brought into harmony with society. 2. According to Maine, a fiction announces openly that a rule of law has been altered. 3. Asquith LJ's dictum requires the consequences of the assumed state of affairs to be imagined as real, unless prohibited. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 and 3 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 restate the passage. Maine's fiction conceals, rather than announces, the alteration.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A omits statement 3, which is correct. Option B includes statement 2, which reverses Maine's definition. Option D includes statement 2, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: 'conceals' becomes 'announces openly'.
questions.language_trick: 'announces openly' against 'conceals, or affects to conceal'.

passages.title: Theories of Justice: Aristotle, Rawls, Nozick, Sen and Access to Justice in India
passages.passage: Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics, distinguished general justice, which is lawfulness, from particular justice, which is distributive, allocating honours and goods according to merit, or corrective, restoring equality after a wrong; like cases are to be treated alike and unlike cases unlike, in proportion to their difference. In A Theory of Justice (1971), John Rawls called justice 'the first virtue of social institutions'. He argued that principles of justice are chosen in an 'original position' behind a 'veil of ignorance', where parties do not know their class, talents or conception of the good. They would choose two principles: equal basic liberties for all, which have priority, and social and economic inequalities arranged so that they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle) and attach to offices open to all under fair equality of opportunity. Robert Nozick, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), replied that justice lies in the process by which holdings arise: a holding is just if justly acquired, justly transferred or rectified for past injustice, and any patterned distribution requires continuous interference with liberty. Amartya Sen's The Idea of Justice (2009) criticised Rawls's search for perfectly just institutions, which he called transcendental institutionalism, and urged comparative reasoning to reduce manifest injustice, using the Sanskrit terms niti, for rules and institutions, and nyaya, for realised justice. The Indian Preamble promises 'JUSTICE, social, economic and political', and Article 39A directs the State to ensure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid. In Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), the Supreme Court, confronted with undertrials languishing in Bihar's jails, held that speedy trial is implicit in Article 21 and that free legal service is an essential ingredient of a reasonable, fair and just procedure. In M.H. Hoskot v. State of Maharashtra (1978), Krishna Iyer J. held that an indigent convict has a right to free legal aid for his appeal.

questions.question: A tribunal orders a wrongdoer to pay compensation so as to restore the victim to his position before the wrong. In Aristotle's classification as described, this is

options.A: corrective justice
options.B: difference-principle justice
options.C: distributive justice
options.D: general justice

questions.explanation: Corrective justice restores equality after a wrong.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is Rawls's principle for social and economic inequalities. Option C allocates honours and goods according to merit. Option D means lawfulness as a whole.
questions.clat_trap: Rawls's term is placed with Aristotle's to tempt a mismatch.

questions.question: A tax-and-transfer scheme raises the position of the least advantaged but increases inequalities between others, while preserving equal basic liberties and fair equality of opportunity. On Rawls as described, the scheme is

options.A: impermissible, since any inequality between persons is unjust in itself
options.B: permissible, as the inequalities benefit the least advantaged most
options.C: impermissible, unless every holding arose by just acquisition and transfer
options.D: permissible even if it curtails basic liberties, as welfare is maximised

questions.explanation: Inequalities are permitted if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged and meet the conditions of liberty and opportunity.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the difference principle. Option C is Nozick's entitlement test, not Rawls's. Option D ignores the priority of liberty.
questions.clat_trap: Rawls and Nozick are opposed on redistribution, so candidates assign one test to the other.

questions.question: A person's wealth was justly acquired and justly transferred. The State taxes it to equalise holdings. On Nozick's theory as described, the taxation

options.A: is justified, since the difference principle demands such redistribution of holdings
options.B: is justified, since the least advantaged would be protected under the veil of ignorance
options.C: is justified, since distributive justice means rectification of every inequality
options.D: infringes his entitlement, since patterns need continuous interference with liberty

questions.explanation: Nozick tests the process: just acquisition and transfer produce just holdings, and patterns require interference.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Rawls's principle, not Nozick's. Option B applies a Rawlsian device, not Nozick's. Option C ignores that rectification applies only to past injustice.
questions.clat_trap: A distributive-justice instinct makes taxation to help the poor look obviously right.

questions.question: Sen's criticism of transcendental institutionalism is that

options.A: searching for perfectly just institutions is unnecessary, and comparative reasoning can reduce manifest injustice
options.B: it ignores the priority that Rawls gave to liberty over equality in his two principles
options.C: it applies Nozick's entitlement theory to the design of institutions instead of using comparison
options.D: it rejects institutions entirely in favour of realised outcomes, treating rules as irrelevant to justice

questions.explanation: Sen urges comparative, realisation-focused reasoning over the search for perfect institutions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is not Sen's point. Option C misdescribes both theories. Option D overstates; Sen uses niti and nyaya together.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates assume that Sen discards institutions altogether.

questions.question: An undertrial has been in custody for years because of delay and cannot afford a lawyer. On the Indian cases in the passage, he can claim

options.A: nothing, since Article 39A is a directive principle and cannot be enforced
options.B: speedy trial and free legal aid as part of a fair procedure under Article 21
options.C: relief only if he is charged with an offence punishable by death
options.D: free legal aid only for an appeal after conviction

questions.explanation: Hussainara Khatoon held that speedy trial is implicit in Article 21 and that free legal service is essential to a fair procedure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores Hussainara Khatoon. Option C adds a limit not in the passage. Option D is the narrower proposition in Hoskot, which does not exhaust the right.
questions.clat_trap: Hoskot, which concerns an appeal, is set against Hussainara to tempt candidates into a narrow reading.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Nozick would reject the difference principle as a requirement of justice. Reason (R): Nozick holds that justice depends on the historical process by which holdings arise, not on patterned outcomes.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Nozick tests process, not pattern; the difference principle is a pattern requirement, so R explains A.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats R as unconnected, though R is the reason for A. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage implies it.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates who see Rawls and Nozick as 'both about fairness' doubt A.

passages.subject_area: Jurisprudence and Constitutional Law (Rule of Law)
passages.title: The Rule of Law: Dicey, Hayek and Raz, and Its Indian Career
passages.passage: A.V. Dicey, in Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), gave three meanings of the rule of law. First, 'the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power', which excludes arbitrariness, prerogative and wide discretionary authority on the part of the government; no man is punishable except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner before the ordinary courts. Second, equality before the law: 'every man, whatever be his rank or condition, is subject to the ordinary law of the realm and amenable to the jurisdiction of the ordinary tribunals'. Dicey therefore regarded the French droit administratif as inconsistent with the rule of law. Third, the constitution is the consequence of the ordinary law of the land, since rights result from judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons. Critics note that Dicey overlooked the wide discretionary powers and administrative tribunals that already existed in English law. F.A. Hayek wrote in The Road to Serfdom that under the rule of law government is bound by rules 'fixed and announced beforehand'. Joseph Raz, in The Rule of Law and Its Virtue (1977), treated it as a political ideal which can be had with or without just law, and distinguished the rule of law from the rule of good law. He listed principles including that laws must be prospective, open and clear, and relatively stable; that the making of particular laws be guided by open, stable, clear and general rules; that the judiciary be independent; that the principles of natural justice be observed; that courts have power of review; that courts be easily accessible; and that the discretion of crime-preventing agencies not be allowed to pervert the law. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court struck down clause (4) of Article 329A, inserted by the 39th Amendment to validate the Prime Minister's election and bar judicial scrutiny, as violating basic features, including the rule of law and free and fair elections. Article 14 of the Constitution forbids the denial of 'equality before the law' (a phrase associated with Dicey) and of 'the equal protection of the laws' (a phrase from American constitutional law).

questions.question: A statute gives an official wide, unreviewable discretion to detain any person he thinks dangerous. On Dicey's first meaning of the rule of law, the statute

options.A: is consistent, so long as detention is reviewed by a specialised administrative tribunal
options.B: conflicts with the rule of law only if the person detained is a foreigner or visitor
options.C: conflicts with the supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power and wide discretion
options.D: is consistent with the rule of law, since it was duly enacted by Parliament

questions.explanation: Dicey's first meaning excludes arbitrariness and wide discretionary authority on the part of the government.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts Dicey's hostility to administrative tribunals. Option B adds a limit absent from Dicey's formulation. Option D ignores the exclusion of wide discretionary authority.
questions.clat_trap: Parliamentary enactment feels like a complete answer, but Dicey's test is the regularity of the law, not its source alone.

questions.question: Dicey regarded the French droit administratif as inconsistent with the rule of law because it

options.A: treats the constitution as the consequence of judicial decisions on private rights
options.B: requires laws to be prospective, open and clear, so that persons can follow them
options.C: allows citizens to sue the State in the ordinary courts like private persons
options.D: subjects officials to a separate system, not to the ordinary law and tribunals

questions.explanation: Dicey's second meaning requires everyone, officials included, to be subject to the ordinary law and tribunals.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Dicey's third meaning, which he approved. Option B is Raz's principle, not Dicey's objection. Option C is the reverse of the French system as Dicey saw it.
questions.clat_trap: Raz's principles and Dicey's meanings are interleaved in the passage.

questions.question: A regime enacts clear, general, prospective and stable laws that harshly burden one minority group, and it has independent courts. On Raz's account as described, the regime

options.A: can satisfy the rule of law while its laws are unjust, as it is not the rule of good law
options.B: cannot satisfy the rule of law, since unjust laws are never law at all in Raz's view
options.C: satisfies the rule of law only if the discrimination is approved by the minority
options.D: cannot satisfy the rule of law, since Dicey requires equality before the law for all

questions.explanation: Raz treats the rule of law as a formal ideal that can be had with or without just law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B states a natural-law claim Raz's view does not make. Option C has no support in the passage. Option D uses Dicey's second meaning against Raz's separate account.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates equate the rule of law with justice, which Raz expressly separates.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the principles of the rule of law attributed to Raz in the passage?

options.A: that laws be prospective, open and clear, so that persons can be guided by them
options.B: that every law must be enacted by a directly elected Parliament
options.C: that the courts be easily accessible to those who seek justice
options.D: that the judiciary be independent of the executive and the legislature

questions.explanation: Raz's list concerns the form and administration of law, not the democratic origin of the enacting body.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is a listed principle. Option C is a listed principle. Option D is a listed principle.
questions.clat_trap: Democratic legislation is associated with the rule of law, so candidates assume it is on Raz's list.

questions.question: A constitutional amendment declares a particular election result valid and bars all judicial scrutiny of it. On Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain as described, such a provision is

options.A: likely to be struck down for violating basic features, including the rule of law
options.B: invalid only because it was introduced by the Prime Minister's party in Parliament
options.C: valid, since an amendment of the Constitution cannot be tested by any court
options.D: valid, if it is passed by the required special majority in both Houses

questions.explanation: The Court struck down Article 329A(4) as violating basic features.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B party origin is not a ground in the passage. Option C contradicts the decision striking down clause (4) of Article 329A. Option D special majority does not cure violation of basic features.
questions.clat_trap: Option B rests on the idea that formal constitutional procedure ends the inquiry.
questions.language_trick: 'basic features' is the limit on amendment.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Raz holds that a legal system which satisfies the rule of law is necessarily just. Reason (R): Raz distinguished the rule of law from the rule of good law.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because Raz says the rule of law can exist without just law; R is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats A as true, though Raz says the rule of law can be had with or without just law. Option B treats A as true, though Raz says the rule of law can be had with or without just law. Option C treats A as true and R as false, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates equate legality with justice.
questions.language_trick: 'necessarily just' against 'with or without just law'.

passages.subject_area: Jurisprudence and Constitutional Law (Positivism and Natural Rights)
passages.title: From Gopalan to Puttaswamy: Positivism and Natural Rights in Article 21
passages.passage: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) read 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 as procedure prescribed by a validly enacted law, rejecting the American 'due process' and the view that 'law' meant principles of natural justice. The Court treated Articles 19, 21 and 22 as separate codes, each a 'silo'. Fazl Ali J. dissented, urging that natural justice formed part of the procedure. R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) rejected the silo view for Articles 19 and 31, holding that the effect of a law, not merely its object, decides which fundamental rights are infringed. In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Bhagwati J. observed that 'equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions and it cannot be cribbed, cabined and confined within traditional and doctrinaire limits', adding that 'from a positivistic point of view, equality is antithetic to arbitrariness'. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), seven judges held that Article 21 requires a procedure that is right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive, and that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive; Bhagwati J. said that 'the principle of reasonableness ... pervades Article 14 like a brooding omnipresence'. In A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), during the Emergency, a majority of four held that, with Article 21 suspended under the Presidential Order, no person could seek habeas corpus to challenge detention, since Article 21 was the sole repository of the right to life and personal liberty. H.R. Khanna J., dissenting, wrote: 'Even in the absence of Article 21 in the Constitution, the State has no power to deprive a person of his life or liberty without the authority of law. This is the essential postulate and basic assumption of the rule of law and not of men in all civilised nations.' In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Bench overruled A.D.M. Jabalpur, holding that life and personal liberty are not creations of the Constitution but inhere in every individual, and that privacy is protected under Articles 14, 19 and 21.

questions.question: The majority view in Gopalan on 'procedure established by law' was that it meant

options.A: a procedure that conforms to principles of natural justice, as Fazl Ali J. urged in dissent
options.B: any procedure prescribed by a validly enacted law, without a test of fairness
options.C: a procedure that satisfies the American standard of due process of law
options.D: a procedure that is right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive

questions.explanation: Gopalan read the phrase as procedure laid down by a valid statute.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Fazl Ali J.'s dissenting view. Option C is the standard the Court rejected. Option D is the Maneka Gandhi standard.
questions.clat_trap: Maneka Gandhi's standard is placed as a distractor to catch candidates who read the later law back.

questions.question: The significance of R.C. Cooper in the line of cases in the passage is that it

options.A: overruled Maneka Gandhi on the relation of Articles 14, 19 and 21 under the silo theory
options.B: rejected the silo view and looked to the effect, not the object, of the law
options.C: upheld Gopalan's reading of 'procedure established by law' as enacted procedure
options.D: held that Article 21 was the sole repository of the right to life and personal liberty

questions.explanation: Cooper held that effect, not object, decides which fundamental rights a law infringes, and so rejected the silos.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A Cooper (1970) predates Maneka Gandhi (1978). Option C Cooper rejected the silo reading associated with Gopalan. Option D is the majority view in Jabalpur.
questions.clat_trap: Dates matter: a 1970 decision cannot overrule a 1978 decision.

questions.question: A law allows the authorities to impound a passport without giving the holder any opportunity of being heard, and the procedure is arbitrary. On Maneka Gandhi as described, the procedure

options.A: is a matter on which the courts cannot inquire, since it is an executive procedure
options.B: fails Article 21, because it is not right, just and fair
options.C: is tested only under Article 19, because passports concern movement
options.D: satisfies Article 21, because it is prescribed by an enacted law

questions.explanation: Maneka Gandhi requires a procedure that is right, just and fair under Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A has no support in the passage. Option C ignores that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive. Option D is the Gopalan view that Maneka Gandhi displaced.
questions.clat_trap: Gopalan's position is attractive to candidates who think a law means any law.

questions.question: Khanna J.'s dissent in A.D.M. Jabalpur is best seen as an expression of a view that

options.A: law is the prediction of what the courts will do in fact, and nothing more than that
options.B: law is a command of the sovereign backed by a sanction, whatever its moral content
options.C: the right to life and liberty rests on the rule of law, not merely on the text of the Constitution
options.D: a right exists only if the Constitution has enacted it, since Article 21 is the sole repository

questions.explanation: Khanna J. said that the State has no power to deprive a person of life or liberty without authority of law even without Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Holmes's predictive theory, which the dissent does not rest upon. Option B is Austin's theory, which the dissent does not rest upon. Option D is the position of the majority.
questions.clat_trap: Positivist labels (Austin, Holmes) are offered as distractors, since the case is about positivism.

questions.question: Puttaswamy repudiates the reasoning of the Jabalpur majority by holding that life and personal liberty

options.A: are confined to citizens and are not available to all persons within the territory
options.B: may be suspended at will once an Emergency is proclaimed by the President
options.C: exist only to the extent that the Constitution confers them by its express text
options.D: are not creations of the Constitution but inhere in every individual as a person

questions.explanation: The nine-judge Bench overruled Jabalpur and held that life and liberty inhere in every individual.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A has no support in the passage. Option B is the consequence that the majority accepted and Puttaswamy rejects. Option C is the Jabalpur majority view.
questions.clat_trap: Distractors state the Jabalpur reasoning.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Gopalan treated Articles 19, 21 and 22 as separate codes. 2. Royappa described equality as a static concept confined within traditional limits. 3. Maneka Gandhi held that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 3 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: 1 and 2 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 restate the passage; Royappa called equality a dynamic concept.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B relies on statement 2, which reverses Royappa. Option C includes statement 2 and omits statement 3. Option D includes statement 2, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: 'dynamic' becomes 'static'.
questions.language_trick: 'cribbed, cabined and confined' is what Royappa rejects.

passages.title: Critical Perspectives: Marxist, Critical Legal Studies and Feminist Jurisprudence
passages.passage: Marx and Engels treated law as part of the superstructure. In the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859), Marx wrote that the relations of production form 'the real foundation, on which rises a legal and political superstructure', and that 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness.' In the Communist Manifesto they told the bourgeoisie: 'Your jurisprudence is but the will of your class made into a law for all'. Later Marxists, such as Pashukanis, argued that the legal form mirrors commodity exchange, and Gramsci and Althusser stressed hegemony and ideological state apparatuses. Critical Legal Studies, which emerged in the United States in the 1970s with Roberto Unger, Duncan Kennedy and Mark Tushnet, built on realism and Marxism: it argued that law is indeterminate because doctrines contain counter-principles that permit opposite results, that legal reasoning is politics by other means, and that liberal legalism legitimises hierarchy. Feminist jurisprudence examines how law embodies male perspectives. Liberal feminists seek equal treatment, cultural feminists, influenced by Carol Gilligan's ethic of care, stress difference, and Catharine MacKinnon's dominance approach holds that sex inequality is a matter of power and not difference, and that the law's neutrality is itself male. In India, in Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008), the Supreme Court struck down a statutory bar on employing women in places serving liquor as resting on paternalistic stereotypes. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), it struck down section 497 of the Indian Penal Code (adultery) as treating the wife as the husband's property and as resting on stereotypes. In Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya (2020), it held that denying permanent commission to women officers on stereotyped notions of capacity violated Articles 14, 15 and 16.

questions.question: In Marx's 1859 formulation, as quoted, law belongs to

options.A: the ideal of justice that stands outside class interests
options.B: the foundation formed by the relations of production
options.C: the superstructure that rises on the economic foundation
options.D: the consciousness that determines social existence

questions.explanation: Marx places legal and political institutions on the superstructure that rises on the real foundation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is not Marx's view. Option B is the economic base and not law. Option D reverses the quoted relation between consciousness and existence.
questions.clat_trap: The base and superstructure are easily reversed.

questions.question: A Critical Legal Studies scholar reads two sets of cases, decided oppositely, each supported by a doctrine in the same branch of law, and each reasoned with equal persuasiveness. This illustrates her claim that

options.A: law is the command of a sovereign backed by a sanction, so that results follow from commands
options.B: law is determinate and always yields a single right answer to every dispute
options.C: law is indeterminate, since doctrines contain counter-principles permitting opposite results
options.D: law is part of the economic foundation of society rather than its superstructure

questions.explanation: CLS holds that counter-principles in doctrine permit opposite results.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is Austin's view. Option B is Dworkin's thesis, not CLS. Option D is a reversal of the Marxist base-superstructure relation.
questions.clat_trap: Dworkin's right-answer thesis appears in other passages and is a tempting wrong match.

questions.question: Catharine MacKinnon's dominance approach, as described, holds that

options.A: women and men differ, and the law should value an ethic of care and relationship
options.B: law is the will of the ruling class made into a law for all, as the Manifesto says
options.C: the law should treat women and men identically wherever possible, ignoring differences
options.D: sex inequality is about power, not difference, and legal neutrality is itself male

questions.explanation: MacKinnon treats sex inequality as power and sees neutrality as male.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the cultural feminist position. Option B is the Marxist claim in the Manifesto. Option C is the liberal feminist position.
questions.clat_trap: Three feminist positions and Marx are listed; each distractor belongs to another.

questions.question: A State bars women from working night shifts in restaurants, on the ground that it is protecting them. On Anuj Garg as described, the bar is

options.A: valid, because Article 15(3) removes all review of laws concerning women
options.B: valid, since protective discrimination in favour of women is always permitted
options.C: invalid only if women's organisations challenge it
options.D: likely to be invalid, as resting on paternalistic stereotypes

questions.explanation: Anuj Garg struck down a bar on women's employment that rested on paternalistic stereotypes.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates Article 15(3), which the passage does not mention as a shield. Option B ignores that Anuj Garg struck down a protective bar. Option C has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A protective purpose sounds benign, and candidates accept it.

questions.question: Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code was struck down in Joseph Shine on the ground, among others, that it

options.A: treated the wife as the husband's property and rested on stereotypes
options.B: punished the wife and not her paramour
options.C: conflicted with Article 15(3), which permits special provisions for women
options.D: was an offence only in the Armed Forces

questions.explanation: The passage says the section treated the wife as property and rested on stereotypes.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B misdescribes the section, which did not punish the wife. Option C misapplies Article 15(3), which is not mentioned in the passage. Option D has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The facts of section 497 are often misremembered, and a distractor reverses who was punished.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Pashukanis argued that the legal form mirrors commodity exchange. Reason (R): Marxists treat law as part of the superstructure.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are in the passage, but R does not explain why Pashukanis linked law to commodity exchange.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats R as the explanation of A, though R states a general Marxist premise and does not itself explain Pashukanis's specific thesis. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Two statements in one paragraph are paired to invite an assumed link.
questions.language_trick: Test whether R explains A, not merely whether R is true.

passages.title: Judges as Lawmakers: Interstitial Legislation, Activism and Restraint
passages.passage: Blackstone's declaratory theory held that judges do not make law but discover it, as 'the oracles of the law'. Bentham compared judge-made law to the way a man makes rules for his dog, waiting until the dog offends and then beating it, and called it 'dog law'. Lord Reid, in 'The Judge as Law Maker' (1972), said that people once thought it almost indecent to suggest that judges make law, but 'we do not believe in fairy tales any more'. Holmes J., dissenting in Southern Pacific Co. v. Jensen (1917), wrote: 'I recognize without hesitation that judges do and must legislate, but they can do so only interstitially; they are confined from molar to molecular motions.' In India, the Supreme Court has issued directions where legislation was absent. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), it laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace, drawing on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women and on Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21, to operate until Parliament legislated; Parliament did so in 2013. In Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998), the Court supervised investigations by the Central Bureau of Investigation through continuing mandamus. Critics speak of judicial overreach. In Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (2008), Katju J. stressed that judges must exercise self-restraint and not take over the functions of the legislature or the executive. In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955), the Court held that the Constitution does not recognise the separation of powers in its absolute rigidity, though the functions of the organs are sufficiently differentiated, and in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the separation of powers was treated as part of the basic structure. Judicial restraint urges deference to the political branches; judicial activism urges that courts use their power to remedy gaps and injustice.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the declaratory theory of adjudication described in the passage?

options.A: judges do not make law but discover it, as oracles of the law
options.B: judges make rules for people as a man makes rules for his dog
options.C: judges legislate, but only interstitially
options.D: judges should defer to the political branches

questions.explanation: Blackstone's declaratory theory says judges discover and do not make law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is Bentham's mocking criticism of the theory. Option C is Holmes's view and the opposite of the declaratory theory. Option D is the doctrine of judicial restraint.
questions.clat_trap: Several statements about judicial role appear, and the criticisms are easily mistaken for the theory.

questions.question: Holmes's statement that judges 'are confined from molar to molecular motions' means that judicial law-making is

options.A: unlimited, since judges may enact sweeping new codes
options.B: forbidden, since judges must only discover the law
options.C: limited to filling gaps and making small adjustments within the existing law
options.D: limited to cases in which the legislature has expressly delegated power

questions.explanation: Interstitial legislation fills gaps in the interstices of existing law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the word confined. Option B is the declaratory theory, which Holmes rejects. Option D has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: 'Legislate' makes the sentence sound broad, but the sentence is about limits.

questions.question: Employees face sexual harassment at work and no statute governs the matter. On Vishaka as described, the Supreme Court may

options.A: lay down guidelines from constitutional articles and conventions to hold the field until legislation
options.B: refuse to act, since only Parliament may make law on workplace harassment and the Court may not fill gaps
options.C: direct the CBI to investigate each complaint under continuing mandamus supervised by the Court
options.D: enact a permanent statute that Parliament may not amend and that overrides all later law

questions.explanation: Vishaka's guidelines held the field until Parliament enacted the 2013 Act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B contradicts Vishaka. Option C describes Vineet Narain, not Vishaka. Option D goes beyond interim guidelines.
questions.clat_trap: Vineet Narain's continuing mandamus is placed next to Vishaka in the passage.

questions.question: Reading Ram Jawaya Kapur and Kesavananda together, which statement about separation of powers in India is correct?

options.A: It is applied in absolute rigidity, with no overlap of functions
options.B: It is not applied rigidly, though it forms part of the basic structure
options.C: It is recognised only for the judiciary and not for the executive
options.D: It is not recognised in India at all

questions.explanation: Ram Jawaya Kapur rejects rigidity; Kesavananda treats the separation of powers as part of the basic structure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts Ram Jawaya Kapur. Option C has no support in the passage. Option D contradicts Kesavananda's treatment of it as basic structure.
questions.clat_trap: Two decisions seem to pull in opposite directions, and candidates choose one.

questions.question: A petition asks the Court to direct the legislature to enact a particular law within six months. On the restraint approach in Aravali Golf Club as described, this request

options.A: would involve the Court taking over the legislature's function, and should be declined
options.B: is justified by Vineet Narain, which gives courts control of legislation
options.C: is justified because Holmes accepted unlimited judicial legislation
options.D: is justified by Vishaka, which allows courts to command Parliament to legislate

questions.explanation: Aravali Golf Club stresses self-restraint and non-encroachment on the legislature.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B Vineet Narain concerned supervising investigations. Option C misreads Holmes, who said judges legislate only interstitially. Option D Vishaka laid down interim guidelines and did not command Parliament.
questions.clat_trap: Vishaka tempts candidates, but it filled a gap and did not order Parliament.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Holmes accepted that judges legislate. Reason (R): Holmes held that judges may legislate without any limit.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true: judges do and must legislate. R is false: he said they legislate only interstitially.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats R as true and as the explanation, though Holmes confined legislation to interstices. Option B treats R as true, though Holmes confined legislation to interstices. Option D treats A as false and R as true, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: R distorts the quotation by dropping 'only interstitially'.

passages.title: Mens Rea, Strict Liability and the Presumption of Fault
passages.passage: The maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea means that an act does not make a person guilty unless his mind is also guilty. Holmes wrote in The Common Law that 'even a dog distinguishes between being stumbled over and being kicked'. Mens rea takes different forms: intention, knowledge, recklessness and negligence. Motive is distinct from intention and is generally irrelevant to liability, though it may be relevant to proof and to sentence. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines terms such as 'dishonestly' and 'fraudulently' in section 2 and keeps general exceptions such as section 14, which protects an act done by a person who by mistake of fact, in good faith, believes himself bound by law to do it, and section 17, which protects an act done by mistake of fact in good faith believing oneself justified by law; mistake of law is no defence, according to the maxim ignorantia juris non excusat. Statutes sometimes impose strict liability, which dispenses with proof of mens rea as to an element of the offence. Courts begin with a presumption that mens rea is required, as in Sherras v. De Rutzen (1895). Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v. Attorney-General of Hong Kong (1985) held that the presumption is particularly strong where the offence is truly criminal, that it is displaced only if the statute clearly or by necessary implication so provides, and that it is displaced only where the statute deals with an issue of social concern and strict liability will promote its objects by encouraging greater vigilance. In India, Nathulal v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1966) held that mens rea is an essential ingredient of a criminal offence unless the statute excludes it expressly or by necessary implication. In State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George (1965), the Supreme Court held that a traveller who carried gold into India in breach of a Reserve Bank notification of which he was unaware was guilty, since the object of the foreign exchange law would be defeated if the offence required knowledge of the notification.

questions.question: Holmes's remark that even a dog distinguishes between being stumbled over and being kicked is meant to illustrate that

options.A: a person is liable for every harm that follows from his acts, whatever his state of mind
options.B: strict liability is the normal rule in criminal law, with mens rea as the exception
options.C: the same physical harm is judged differently according to the mental state of its author
options.D: motive is the principal test of criminal liability, since motive reveals the guilty mind

questions.explanation: The dog distinguishes an accidental from an intentional contact, which is the role of mens rea.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the point about distinguishing intention from accident. Option B contradicts the presumption of mens rea. Option D motive is generally irrelevant to liability, according to the passage.
questions.clat_trap: 'Motive' and 'intention' are often confused, and the distractor exploits it.

questions.question: A man steals medicine to give it to a dying relative who cannot afford it. His motive is laudable. On the passage, his motive

options.A: is generally irrelevant to liability, though relevant to sentence
options.B: excuses him, because motive is the real test of mens rea in criminal law
options.C: excuses him, because necessity applies automatically to every theft of medicine
options.D: makes his act one of strict liability, since the motive is not part of the offence

questions.explanation: Motive is distinct from intention and does not by itself negate liability.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats motive as the test of mens rea. Option C has no support in the passage. Option D confuses motive with strict liability.
questions.clat_trap: A sympathetic motive tempts candidates to excuse, forgetting the distinction.

questions.question: A statute on adulterated food, silent on mens rea, makes it an offence to sell adulterated food. A shopkeeper sells adulterated sweets unknowingly. On Gammon as described, the offence

options.A: is automatically one of strict liability, since all regulatory offences dispense with mens rea whatever the statute says
options.B: is not an offence at all unless the shopkeeper knew of the adulteration at the time of the sale
options.C: may be treated as strict liability if the statute so implies by necessary implication and strictness will promote its objects
options.D: can never be one of strict liability, since the presumption of mens rea is absolute in all cases

questions.explanation: Gammon allows the presumption to be displaced for matters of social concern where strict liability promotes the statute's objects.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the conditions in Gammon. Option B assumes the presumption cannot be displaced. Option D ignores that the presumption can be displaced.
questions.clat_trap: Both extremes ('always' and 'never') are offered, whereas the rule is conditional.

questions.question: The difference in outcome between Nathulal and Mayer Hans George is best explained by the view that in

options.A: both cases the Court held that motive, rather than intention or knowledge, decides liability
options.B: George the Court held that mens rea is always essential, even where the object of the law would be defeated
options.C: George the Court found, from the object of the law, that mens rea was impliedly excluded, unlike Nathulal
options.D: Nathulal the Court held that strict liability is the general rule in India unless a statute requires mens rea

questions.explanation: Nathulal states the presumption; George shows it displaced by the object of the foreign exchange law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is not the reasoning of either case. Option B contradicts the conviction of a traveller who was unaware of the notification. Option D contradicts the holding that mens rea is essential unless excluded.
questions.clat_trap: The two cases are described in one breath, and candidates assume they conflict.

questions.question: Which of the following is protected under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita provisions described in the passage?

options.A: a person who, by a mistake of law, honestly believes that the law does not forbid his conduct
options.B: a person who knows the law but believes that it is unjust and so refuses to obey it
options.C: a person who acts out of a laudable motive but with full knowledge of all the facts
options.D: a police officer who in good faith, by mistake of fact, believes himself bound by law to arrest

questions.explanation: Sections 14 and 17 protect mistake of fact in good faith, not mistake of law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is not protected, since mistake of law is no defence. Option B is not a mistake of fact. Option C has no protection from motive alone.
questions.clat_trap: Fact and law mistakes are placed side by side.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Mayer Hans George, the traveller was held guilty though he was unaware of the notification. Reason (R): The Court held that mens rea was not required for the offence in that context.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court convicted because it held that knowledge of the notification was not required, so R explains A.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats R as unconnected, though R is the Court's reason for A. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates who learned Nathulal doubt that George could convict without mens rea.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: General Part)
passages.title: BNS, 2023: Punishments, Community Service, Commutation and General Exceptions
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860 with effect from 1 July 2024. Section 4 lists the punishments: death; imprisonment for life; imprisonment, rigorous or simple; forfeiture of property; fine; and community service, which is work that the court may order a convict to perform as punishment for the benefit of the community, without remuneration. Community service is prescribed for six offences: a public servant unlawfully engaging in trade (section 202), non-attendance in obedience to an order from a public servant (section 209), an attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain the exercise of a lawful power (section 226), theft of property worth less than five thousand rupees by a first offender who restores it (section 303(2)), misconduct in public by a drunken person (section 355), and defamation (section 356(2)).
