Section 5 allows the appropriate Government to commute a sentence without the offender's consent, in accordance with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita; a sentence of death may be commuted only to imprisonment for life, and a sentence of imprisonment for life only to imprisonment of not less than seven years. Section 2 defines a child as a person under eighteen and provides that 'gender' includes transgender persons. Among the general exceptions, section 19 protects an act done without criminal intention, knowing that it is likely to cause harm, in good faith, to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property; whether the harm to be avoided is of such a nature and so imminent as to justify the risk is a question of fact. Section 20 protects a child under seven absolutely. Section 21 protects a child above seven and under twelve who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of his conduct. Section 22 protects a person who, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law; the burden of proving the defence lies on the accused, who need only establish it on a preponderance of probabilities. English law refuses necessity as a defence to murder (R v. Dudley and Stephens, 1884).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an offence for which the BNS prescribes community service, as described in the passage?

options.A: misconduct in public by a drunken person
options.B: non-attendance in obedience to an order from a public servant
options.C: robbery
options.D: defamation

questions.explanation: The passage lists six offences, none of which is robbery.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is listed, under section 355. Option B is listed, under section 209. Option D is listed, under section 356(2).
questions.clat_trap: Community service is new and sounds suitable only for petty wrongs, so candidates may think it covers a wide range.

questions.question: A State Government wishes to commute a sentence of death. Under the BNS and the BNSS as described, it may commute the sentence only to

options.A: fine
options.B: rigorous imprisonment for fourteen years
options.C: imprisonment of not less than seven years
options.D: imprisonment for life

questions.explanation: Death may be commuted only to imprisonment for life; life imprisonment may be commuted to not less than seven years.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is not a permitted commutation of death. Option B was possible under the older law, but the passage permits commutation of death only to life imprisonment. Option C is the floor for commuting a sentence of life imprisonment, not death.
questions.clat_trap: The seven-year floor for life sentences is placed in a distractor for death sentences.
questions.language_trick: 'only to' marks the single permitted step.

questions.question: A bus driver whose brakes suddenly fail steers into a lone parked scooter, injuring its owner, to avoid ploughing into a crowded queue of passengers. He acted in good faith and without criminal intention. On section 19 as described, he

options.A: commits no offence if the harm avoided was so imminent as to justify the risk, a question of fact
options.B: is guilty, because English law refuses necessity as a defence to a charge of causing harm
options.C: is protected automatically, because good faith ends any inquiry into the imminence of the harm
options.D: is guilty, because knowledge that harm is likely is by itself an offence under the BNS

questions.explanation: Section 19 protects an act done to avoid other harm if the harm was so imminent as to justify the risk, a question of fact.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies the rule on murder in Dudley and Stephens to a case of lesser harm. Option C ignores that the justification of the risk is a question of fact. Option D ignores the good-faith, no-criminal-intention exception.
questions.clat_trap: The Dudley and Stephens reference is a distractor drawn from a murder case.

questions.question: A ten-year-old, who fully understands the nature and wrongfulness of the act, takes a neighbour's bicycle intending to keep it. On sections 20 and 21 as described, the child

options.A: has no protection under section 21 as he has sufficient maturity, and section 20 covers only children under seven
options.B: is protected under section 22, since a child of that age is presumed to be of unsound mind in law
options.C: is protected under section 21 automatically, since every child under twelve is protected whatever his maturity
options.D: is protected absolutely under section 20, since the protection extends to every child under twelve years of age

questions.explanation: Between seven and twelve, protection depends on want of sufficient maturity, which this child lacks.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B unsoundness of mind is not presumed from age. Option C section 21 requires want of sufficient maturity of understanding. Option D section 20 covers only a child under seven.
questions.clat_trap: Age is the visible fact, and candidates ignore the maturity condition.
questions.language_trick: 'under seven' against 'above seven and under twelve'.

questions.question: An accused knows that he is killing a person but, because of a delusion caused by unsoundness of mind, does not know that the act is wrong or contrary to law. On section 22 as described,

options.A: the defence is available, and the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt
options.B: the defence is available only if he has been treated in a mental hospital before
options.C: the defence is available if he proves it on a preponderance of probabilities
options.D: the defence is unavailable, since he knew the nature of the act

questions.explanation: Section 22 protects incapacity to know the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law, and the accused carries the burden on probabilities.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A misplaces the burden, which is on the accused. Option B adds a condition not in the passage. Option D overlooks the alternative limb: incapacity to know that the act is wrong or contrary to law.
questions.clat_trap: The knowledge of the nature of the act is a decoy; the second limb of the test applies.
questions.language_trick: 'or that it is wrong or contrary to law' is disjunctive.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Section 4 of the BNS lists forfeiture of property and community service among the punishments. 2. Under section 2, 'gender' includes transgender persons. 3. Section 20 protects absolutely a child under twelve years. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 2 only
options.B: 1 and 2 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 restate the passage; section 20 protects a child under seven.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A omits statement 1, which is correct. Option C includes statement 3 and omits statement 2. Option D includes statement 3, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: 'seven' is replaced by 'twelve', the upper limit of section 21.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: Joint and Inchoate Liability)
passages.title: Common Intention, Common Object, Abetment, Conspiracy and Attempt under the BNS
passages.passage: Section 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly section 34 of the Indian Penal Code) provides that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of them is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. It creates no substantive offence but states a rule of joint liability. Common intention requires a prearranged plan, a meeting of minds, though the plan may be formed on the spur of the moment, and participation in the criminal act: Mahbub Shah v. King-Emperor (1945) and Pandurang v. State of Hyderabad (1955). In Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King-Emperor (1925), the Privy Council held liable for murder a man who stood outside a post office while his companions entered and shot the postmaster, remarking that 'they also serve who only stand and wait'. Section 190 (formerly section 149) makes every member of an unlawful assembly guilty of an offence committed in prosecution of the common object, or which the members knew to be likely to be committed; an unlawful assembly requires five or more persons, and membership with knowledge of the common object suffices, without any personal act. Abetment is defined in section 45: a person abets the doing of a thing who instigates it, or engages in a conspiracy for its doing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of the conspiracy, or intentionally aids it. Criminal conspiracy under section 61 is an agreement to do an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means; except where the agreement is to commit an offence, some act besides the agreement must be done in pursuance of it. An attempt to commit an offence is punished under section 62 with up to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the offence, or with fine, or with both.

questions.question: Section 3(5) of the BNS is best described as

options.A: a substantive offence punishable in its own right
options.B: a rule that requires no participation in the criminal act
options.C: a rule of joint liability that creates no separate offence
options.D: a rule that applies only to assemblies of five or more persons

questions.explanation: Section 3(5) states a rule of joint liability for an act done in furtherance of the common intention of all.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the statement that it creates no substantive offence. Option B contradicts the requirement of participation. Option D confuses it with section 190.
questions.clat_trap: Common intention and common object are routinely confused.

questions.question: A stands outside a bank, armed, as a lookout, under a prearranged plan, while his companions enter and, in the course of the robbery, kill the cashier. On the passage, A is

options.A: liable only if he himself fired a shot or struck the fatal blow inside the bank
options.B: liable for the killing under section 3(5), since by standing guard he took part in the plan
options.C: not liable, since he did not enter the bank or himself commit the killing of the cashier
options.D: liable only as an abettor of the killing, and not as a principal offender in it

questions.explanation: Barendra Kumar Ghosh holds that those who stand and wait participate in the act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A makes personal commission a condition, which section 3(5) does not require. Option C contradicts the Barendra Kumar Ghosh reasoning. Option D ignores that joint liability treats each as if he had done the act alone.
questions.clat_trap: 'Mere presence' arguments are attractive to candidates who think a bystander is not liable.
questions.language_trick: 'they also serve who only stand and wait'.

questions.question: Four persons, acting on a prearranged plan, beat X to death. Section 190 is not available against them because

options.A: an unlawful assembly needs five or more persons, though section 3(5) may apply on common intention
options.B: no liability can arise in the absence of an unlawful assembly, whatever the plan of the four
options.C: common intention and common object are the same thing, and both are absent on these facts
options.D: section 190 requires the plan to have been made at least a day before the act was done

questions.explanation: Section 190 depends on an unlawful assembly of five or more persons, whereas section 3(5) applies to several persons sharing a common intention.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores section 3(5), which applies to several persons. Option C treats the two concepts as identical, contrary to the passage. Option D invents a timing rule.
questions.clat_trap: The number requirement is the distinguishing feature, and it is hidden in the facts.

questions.question: A and B agree to commit an offence, such as robbery, and do nothing further. On section 61 as described,

options.A: they are guilty of attempt under section 62, since they have planned the robbery together
options.B: there is no criminal conspiracy until some act besides the agreement is done by one of them
options.C: their agreement alone is a criminal conspiracy, as it is an agreement to commit an offence
options.D: they are guilty of abetment by conspiracy, since abetment by conspiracy needs no act at all

questions.explanation: For an agreement to commit an offence, the agreement alone is enough; the overt-act requirement applies to other illegal agreements.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A an agreement alone is not an attempt. Option B applies the overt-act requirement that the passage excludes for agreements to commit offences. Option D abetment by conspiracy requires an act or illegal omission in pursuance of the conspiracy.
questions.clat_trap: The overt-act proviso is easily over-applied, and abetment by conspiracy adds a further requirement.
questions.language_trick: 'except where the agreement is to commit an offence'.

questions.question: A and B conspire to poison C, but no act is done in pursuance of the conspiracy. On section 45 as described,

options.A: A and B have abetted by conspiracy, since a conspiracy for the doing exists
options.B: A and B have attempted murder, since they have agreed on the use of poison
options.C: A and B have not abetted by conspiracy, though a criminal conspiracy is made out
options.D: A and B have committed no offence of any kind, since no harm has been done

questions.explanation: Abetment by conspiracy requires an act or illegal omission in pursuance of the conspiracy; conspiracy to commit an offence does not.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overlooks the requirement of an act or illegal omission in pursuance of the conspiracy. Option B agreement is not an attempt. Option D ignores section 61.
questions.clat_trap: Conspiracy and abetment by conspiracy overlap in language but differ in the act requirement.
questions.language_trick: 'if an act or illegal omission takes place'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Under section 190, a member of an unlawful assembly may be liable though he did no act himself in the offence. Reason (R): Section 190 applies to an assembly of any two or more persons.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true because membership with knowledge of the common object suffices; R is false because five or more persons are required.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats R as true and as the explanation, though an unlawful assembly requires five or more persons. Option B treats R as true, though an unlawful assembly requires five or more persons. Option D treats A as false and R as true, reversing both.
questions.clat_trap: R confuses section 190 with section 3(5), which applies to several persons.
questions.language_trick: 'any two or more' against 'five or more'.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: Offences against the Human Body)
passages.title: Culpable Homicide, Murder, Group Murder and Death by Negligence under the BNS
passages.passage: The BNS retains the structure of the Indian Penal Code on homicide. Section 100 defines culpable homicide, and section 101 provides that culpable homicide is murder if the act is done with the intention of causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause death, or of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or with the knowledge that it is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death. Exceptions, including grave and sudden provocation, exceeding the right of private defence, and sudden fight, reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. In Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (1958), the Supreme Court held that for the third clause the prosecution must prove that a bodily injury was present, that it was intentionally inflicted, and that it was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; it is then murder, though the accused did not intend to cause death. Section 103(1) punishes murder with death or imprisonment for life, and fine. Section 103(2), a new provision aimed at mob lynching, provides that where a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of the group is punishable with death or imprisonment for life, and fine. Section 106(1) punishes causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide with imprisonment of up to five years and fine, but where the act is done by a registered medical practitioner in the course of a medical procedure, the imprisonment may extend only to two years. In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005), the Court held that a doctor is criminally liable only for gross negligence, and not for mere lack of reasonable care or an error of judgment, and that a private complaint should not be entertained without prima facie evidence in the form of a credible opinion of another competent doctor.

questions.question: A, deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation given by B, kills B. On the passage, A is guilty of

options.A: murder, punishable under section 103(1) with death or imprisonment for life and fine
options.B: causing death by negligence under section 106(1), since no intention to kill is shown
options.C: no offence, since grave and sudden provocation is a complete defence to any charge
options.D: culpable homicide not amounting to murder, since the provocation exception applies

questions.explanation: Grave and sudden provocation is an exception that reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the exception that reduces murder to culpable homicide. Option B A acted intentionally, not rashly or negligently. Option C the exception reduces the offence but does not remove liability.
questions.clat_trap: 'Exception' invites candidates to think that it excuses entirely.
questions.language_trick: 'reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder'.

questions.question: A intentionally stabs V in the abdomen with a spear. The wound is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and V dies. A says he never intended to kill. On Virsa Singh as described, A is

options.A: guilty of grievous hurt only, since the injury is classed as grievous hurt and V died of its consequences
options.B: not guilty, since he lacked knowledge that death would follow from the wound he inflicted
options.C: guilty of murder, since the injury was intentionally inflicted and sufficient to cause death, whatever he intended
options.D: guilty of culpable homicide only, since he did not intend to cause the death of V

questions.explanation: Virsa Singh requires intention to inflict the injury and objective sufficiency to cause death; intention to kill is unnecessary.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores that death was caused. Option B the test is intention to inflict the injury, not knowledge of its fatal effect. Option D demands an intention to kill, which the third clause does not require.
questions.clat_trap: The accused's plea that he did not intend death invites the wrong conclusion.
questions.language_trick: 'intentionally inflicted' and 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature'.

questions.question: Four men beat a man to death solely because of his language. On section 103(2) as described,

options.A: section 103(2) applies, since the discriminatory ground alone suffices and the number of persons is irrelevant
options.B: the offence is only causing death by negligence, since no group offence is made out
options.C: each of the four must necessarily be sentenced to death, since the killing was motivated by language
options.D: not attracted, since the group has fewer than five persons; section 103(1) applies if murder is made out

questions.explanation: Section 103(2) needs a group of five or more persons acting in concert on a listed ground.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the requirement of five or more persons. Option B the facts show an intentional beating. Option C section 103(1) permits death or life imprisonment.
questions.clat_trap: The facts match the ground but not the number, and the number is the trap.

questions.question: A surgeon follows a recognised procedure and the patient dies from a known complication. A private complaint alleges negligence under section 106(1). On Jacob Mathew as described,

options.A: criminal law does not apply to doctors at all, who are answerable only in tort for the death of a patient
options.B: section 106(1) applies automatically, since death resulted from a medical procedure performed by the accused
options.C: criminal liability needs gross negligence, and no complaint should proceed without a credible medical opinion
options.D: the surgeon must be arrested immediately so that the evidence of the procedure is preserved for trial

questions.explanation: Jacob Mathew requires gross negligence and prima facie medical opinion before a private complaint proceeds.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overstates; criminal liability exists for gross negligence. Option B ignores the gross negligence requirement. Option D has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A death in a hospital suggests liability, and candidates skip the gross negligence standard.

questions.question: A registered medical practitioner is convicted under section 106(1) of causing death by a negligent act in the course of a medical procedure. The maximum imprisonment is

options.A: seven years
options.B: two years, with fine
options.C: five years, the general maximum in section 106(1)
options.D: ten years

questions.explanation: The proviso reduces the maximum to two years for a registered medical practitioner acting in a medical procedure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is not stated in the passage. Option C applies to cases outside the medical procedure proviso. Option D is not stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The general maximum of five years is stated first and is the tempting answer.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. Under section 101, murder requires an intention to cause death in every case. 2. Section 103(2) applies to a group of five or more persons acting in concert on a prohibited ground. 3. In Virsa Singh, intention to inflict the injury, and not to cause death, was held to suffice under the third clause. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 3 only
options.B: 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Section 101 has four limbs and does not require an intention to kill in every case; statements 2 and 3 restate the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement 1, which is false. Option B omits statement 2, which is correct. Option D includes statement 1, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: 'in every case' converts the first limb into the only limb.
questions.language_trick: 'in every case' is the extreme qualifier.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita: Offences against Woman and Child)
passages.title: BNS Chapter V: Rape, Harassment, Stalking and Matrimonial Offences
passages.passage: Chapter V of the BNS, 'Of Offences Against Woman and Child', opens with section 63 on rape. Consent is an unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, and a woman who does not physically resist is not, by that fact alone, to be regarded as consenting. The age of consent is eighteen. Exception 2 provides that sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape; in Independent Thought v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court read down the corresponding exception in the Indian Penal Code so that intercourse with a wife below eighteen is rape. The exception for adult wives remains under challenge. Section 64 punishes rape with rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, which may extend to life, and fine. Section 65 provides not less than twenty years, up to life, for rape of a woman under sixteen, and punishment up to death for rape of a woman under twelve. Section 66 provides death, or not less than twenty years up to life, where rape causes death or a persistent vegetative state. Section 70(1) provides not less than twenty years, up to life, for gang rape, and section 70(2) provides life imprisonment or death for gang rape of a woman under eighteen. Among other offences, section 74 punishes assault or criminal force to a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, section 75 sexual harassment, section 77 voyeurism, section 78 stalking, which includes following a woman or contacting her despite her clear indication of disinterest and monitoring her use of the internet or email, and section 79 words, gestures or acts intended to insult the modesty of a woman. Section 80 punishes dowry death, where a woman dies otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of marriage and soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment for dowry, with imprisonment of not less than seven years, which may extend to life. Section 85 punishes cruelty by a husband or his relatives, and section 86 defines cruelty.

questions.question: A woman, threatened by the accused, neither resists nor speaks. The accused says that she did not object. On section 63 as described, her failure to resist

options.A: does not by itself amount to consent
options.B: amounts to consent, since consent need not be communicated in any form
options.C: amounts to consent unless she proves that she physically resisted
options.D: is irrelevant, since the age of consent is the only test

questions.explanation: Section 63 requires an unequivocal voluntary agreement and says non-resistance alone is not consent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B contradicts the requirement of an unequivocal communicated agreement. Option C reverses the rule on non-resistance. Option D ignores the definition of consent for adult women.
questions.clat_trap: The popular belief that silence is acquiescence is placed in the distractors.

questions.question: A man has intercourse without her consent with his wife, who is seventeen. On the passage, the intercourse is

options.A: rape only if the wife complains to the police within one year of the intercourse
options.B: not rape, since sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife is never rape in law
options.C: not rape, since the wife's age is irrelevant once the marriage is valid in law
options.D: rape, as Exception 2 protects marital intercourse only with a wife aged eighteen or above

questions.explanation: Exception 2 is confined to wives not under eighteen, and Independent Thought read down the older exception on the same lines.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a time condition. Option B ignores the age limit in Exception 2. Option C ignores the age limit.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates recall that marital rape is excepted and forget the age condition.
questions.language_trick: 'not being under eighteen years of age'.

questions.question: Five persons commit gang rape of a seventeen-year-old girl. The punishment provided under the BNS, as described, is

options.A: imprisonment for life or death, under section 70(2)
options.B: death alone, with no alternative
options.C: not less than ten years, up to life, under section 64
options.D: not less than twenty years, up to life, under section 70(1)

questions.explanation: Gang rape of a woman under eighteen falls under section 70(2).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B section 70(2) provides life imprisonment or death. Option C applies to ordinary rape and not to gang rape of a minor. Option D applies to gang rape of a woman generally, but section 70(2) applies where she is under eighteen.
questions.clat_trap: Three provisions with different minimum terms are placed side by side.

questions.question: A repeatedly follows a woman and monitors her email, despite her clear indication of disinterest. The offence on the passage is

options.A: insulting the modesty of a woman under section 79
options.B: assault with intent to outrage modesty under section 74
options.C: voyeurism under section 77
options.D: stalking under section 78

questions.explanation: Section 78 covers following, contacting despite disinterest, and monitoring of internet or email use.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A concerns words, gestures or acts intended to insult modesty. Option B requires assault or criminal force, which is not described. Option C concerns watching or capturing a private act, not following and monitoring.
questions.clat_trap: Several offences in the same chapter involve intrusion on a woman, and candidates choose the nearest.
questions.language_trick: 'monitoring her use of the internet or email'.

questions.question: A wife dies of burns in unnatural circumstances five years after marriage. There is evidence that soon before her death she was harassed for dowry by her husband. On the passage,

options.A: only cruelty under section 85 applies, since death by burns excludes a dowry death charge
options.B: the offence is only insulting her modesty under section 79, with no dowry offence
options.C: the husband is liable for dowry death under section 80, punishable with seven years to life
options.D: section 80 is not applicable, since death must occur within three years of marriage

questions.explanation: Section 80 applies to unnatural death within seven years of marriage with proof of dowry-related harassment soon before death.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores death otherwise than under normal circumstances. Option B is unrelated to the facts. Option D the period is seven years.
questions.clat_trap: Candidates import the three-year period from other contexts.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Under the BNS, the age of consent is eighteen. Reason (R): In Independent Thought, the Supreme Court read down the exception in the Indian Penal Code for intercourse with a wife below eighteen.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A; it concerns the marital exception.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats R as the explanation of A, though R concerns a particular judicial reading of an exception and does not explain the age of consent. Option C treats R as false, though the passage states it. Option D treats A as false, though the passage states it.
questions.clat_trap: Two related statements are linked by subject-matter, which invites an assumed causal link.
questions.language_trick: Test whether R explains A, not merely whether R is true.

passages.title: BNSS, 2023: Arrest, Undertrial Bail, Forensics, Attachment and Victims
passages.passage: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), in force from 1 July 2024, replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Under section 35, where arrest is not required, the police issue a notice directing the person to appear; and for an offence punishable with imprisonment of less than three years, a person who is infirm or above sixty years of age may be arrested only with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police. Section 479 deals with undertrial detention. An undertrial who has been detained for up to one-half of the maximum imprisonment for the offence is to be released on bail, and a first-time offender, who has never been convicted, on completing one-third. The section does not apply to an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or to a person facing proceedings in more than one case, and the jail superintendent must apply to the court when the period is complete. In Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (2024), the Supreme Court directed that section 479 benefits undertrials in pending cases, even where they were arrested before 1 July 2024. Section 105 requires the search of premises and the seizure of property to be recorded by audio-video means. Section 176(3) requires a forensic expert to visit the scene of an offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more, to collect forensic evidence. Section 107 empowers a court, on the application of a police officer with the approval of a superior police officer, to attach and forfeit proceeds of crime. The Sanhita fixes time limits: a judgment is to be pronounced within forty-five days of the conclusion of arguments, and charges are to be framed within sixty days of the first hearing on charge. It also strengthens the position of the victim, requiring the police to inform the victim of the progress of the investigation within ninety days, and requiring that the victim be heard before the prosecution is withdrawn.

questions.question: A first-time offender is an undertrial for an offence punishable with a maximum of six years' imprisonment, and has been detained for two years. On section 479 as described, he is

options.A: entitled to bail, having completed one-third of the maximum term as a first-time offender
options.B: not entitled until he completes three years, which is one-half of the maximum term
options.C: entitled only after he has been convicted and has appealed against the conviction
options.D: not entitled, since the offence is punishable with imprisonment of more than one year

questions.explanation: A first-time offender who has completed one-third of the maximum term (two years of six) is entitled to release on bail, subject to the exceptions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies the general one-half rule and ignores the first-time offender rule. Option C has no support in the passage. Option D invents a threshold.
questions.clat_trap: The one-half rule is stated first, and candidates miss the shorter period for first-time offenders.

questions.question: An undertrial accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment for life has been in custody for more than half of the maximum period for which he could be sentenced. On section 479 as described,

options.A: section 479 does not apply to him, as the offence is punishable with imprisonment for life
options.B: he must be released on bail as of right on completing one-half of the maximum term
options.C: the jail superintendent may release him without any application to the court at all
options.D: he must be released on bail as of right on completing one-third of the maximum term

questions.explanation: The section excludes offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the exclusion for offences punishable with death or life. Option C misdescribes the superintendent's duty, which is to apply to the court. Option D applies the first-time offender rule to an excluded offence.
questions.clat_trap: The facts mention 'more than half', pointing to release, but the exclusion defeats it.

questions.question: A sixty-five-year-old woman is accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment of two years, and the police wish to arrest her. On section 35 as described, the arrest may be made

options.A: only on a warrant issued by the Supreme Court
options.B: without any permission, since arrest powers are unrestricted for offences below three years
options.C: only after she has been convicted of a similar offence earlier
options.D: only with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police

questions.explanation: Section 35 requires prior permission of an officer not below Deputy Superintendent of Police for the infirm and those above sixty in the stated category.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A has no support in the passage. Option B ignores the special protection. Option C has no support in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A minor offence suggests that no safeguard is needed.
questions.language_trick: 'infirm or above sixty' and 'less than three years'.

questions.question: A police officer investigates an offence punishable with imprisonment of ten years. On section 176(3) as described, he

options.A: may arrange it only if the Magistrate has ordered a forensic visit in writing
options.B: must ensure that a forensic expert visits the scene and collects evidence
options.C: may call a forensic expert at his discretion, depending on the nature of the case
options.D: need do so only where the offence is punishable with death or imprisonment for life

questions.explanation: Section 176(3) requires a forensic expert to visit the scene for offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds a condition not in the passage. Option C makes the visit optional, contrary to the requirement. Option D adds a limit absent from the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'requires' is easily read as 'permits'.

questions.question: Police search premises and seize a laptop. On section 105 as described, the search and seizure

options.A: may be conducted only in the presence of a Magistrate
options.B: must be recorded by audio-video means
options.C: need be recorded only if the premises belong to a woman
options.D: need not be recorded if two independent witnesses are present

questions.explanation: Section 105 requires audio-video recording of search and seizure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A has no support in the passage. Option C adds a limit absent from the passage. Option D makes witnesses a substitute for recording, which the passage does not.
questions.clat_trap: Independent witnesses are familiar from the older law, tempting candidates to treat them as a substitute.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. 1. In Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (2024), the Supreme Court extended the benefit of section 479 to undertrials in pending cases. 2. Section 479 benefits an undertrial accused of an offence punishable with death. 3. Section 107 permits attachment and forfeiture of proceeds of crime on the order of a court. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 2 and 3 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 restate the passage; section 479 excludes offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement 2, which contradicts the exclusion. Option B includes statement 2 and omits statement 1. Option D includes statement 2, which is false.
questions.clat_trap: The exclusion in the section is reversed in statement 2.
